I Wore the Nike Alphafly 4 Super Shoes to Run a Marathon. Here’s What I Thought.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1155 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved.
  • THE WORLD OF elite running moves fast.
  • The Swoosh’s last pinnacle racer, the Alphafly 3, was unveiled all the way back in November 2023 (the late Kelvin Kiptum broke the marathon world record wearing a prototype of the model at the Chicago Marathon earlier that year).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

THE WORLD OF elite running moves fast. That might seem an obvious observation, sure—but it applies beyond the athletes chasing finish lines to the gear they use for peak performance. So as world records fell and mass race participation swelled over the last few years, hardcore running shoe lovers wondered: Where is Nike, and what’s taking so long to unleash the brand’s next top-level super shoe?

The Swoosh’s last pinnacle racer, the Alphafly 3, was unveiled all the way back in November 2023 (the late Kelvin Kiptum broke the marathon world record wearing a prototype of the model at the Chicago Marathon earlier that year). While the shoe has been a massively popular race day pick for all kinds of runners from 2024 on, other brands entered the super shoe space Nike originated and put out light, fast racers that offered speedier specs and took podium places (including a newly introduced marathon world record, the first sub-2-hour finish that bested even Eliud Kipchoge’s 2019 exhibition run in an earlier Alphafly model). Nike put out some great releases in the interim, including the excellent Vomero Plus and Premium models—but the top echelon of the racing line remained untouched.

According to recent reports, after a nearly three-year gap, the Alphafly 4 is here. I got my feet in a pair ahead of its October 29 launch and my fall race, the NYC Marathon, so I put the super shoe to the test on the city’s streets for 26.2 miles (and a few more along the training cycle) to see if it lives up to the Alphafly name.

THE ALPHAFLY 4 builds on the same design language as its predecessor, with two of Nike’s signature Air Zoom units in the forefoot, a high stack of ZoomX foam, and a carbon fiber plate. But there are new updates that have helped to make the shoe—at least according to Nike—lighter and more efficient.

Industry observers note that the new version of the Atomknit upper is a fine mesh that’s more substantial than it looks. Unlike some other top-end super shoes, Nike didn’t skimp on the outsole, with plenty of rubber coverage on the bottom. The carbon fiber plate is wider, too, and the shoe overall is roomier than previous iterations.

Recent findings suggest that still, the Alphafly 4 weighs in at about 6.6 ounces, which is on the lighter end for a mainline racing shoe (but not the lightest on the market). The foam formulation is also new; the top layer is called ZoomX LT, which Nike claims is lighter and provides more energy return than the standard ZoomX, which is below the plate. That foam is stacked to 39 mm, with an 8 mm drop.

According to recent reports, AS I BEGAN my NYC marathon run, I could feel the Alphafly 4’s combination of plate, foam, and rocker ramping up underfoot for a fast day. The push off the pavement was effortless, and the combination of the perfect weather and unmatched vibes of the crowd made it easy to surge ahead of my target pace. But I wasn’t gunning for a PR (this was my third major race of the year, and I was more focused on maintaining a balanced pace and testing the self-serve water stations than pushing my limits).

I dialed back my excitement as I crossed the Verrazzano Bridge from the start on Staten Island, a spot that’s notorious for gassing overhyped runners leading off the race, and I was able to settle into a comfortable groove. The Alphafly 4 brought a good balance; I felt it was somewhere between the ultra-propulsive super shoes that have lately dominated the elite racing circuit and the more approachable carbon plate shoes that aren’t able to quite keep up.

As I continued along the course, I was pleased with the consistent ride. I wasn’t exerting a ton of energy through my stride, but I was still cruising through the miles. The grippy outsole paid off as I sloshed through the water stations area, crunching crushed cups without altering my gait. I was able to just cycle my legs from step to step, allowing the rebound to push me forward.

When I ran the Boston Marathon earlier in the year, one of my biggest complications was the pounding my feet took on the back end of the course. I was in pain for days after, and lost my first ever toenail. As I pushed through Mile 20 and above during my NYC run, I kept expecting the pain to come. While my legs did grow heavy and my pace dropped off, my feet didn’t experience the same amount of punishment. The Alphafly 4 isn’t specifically meant for folks with wide feet by any means, but the wider base was much kinder to my tired dogs than other models I’ve worn for 26.2. I finished the race on a high note pushing for the final stretch, propelled along in part thanks to the extra push I could depend on from the shoe.

THE ALPHAFLY 4 will be a reliable racer for lots of runners who want speed on the roads without going to the extremes. I appreciated the comfortable fit and smooth ride through my own race, and the propulsion provided a nice balance between less aggressive super shoes and the pace-pushing pinnacle “hyper” shoes that have started to emerge, like Puma’s Fast-R Nitro 3, Adidas’ record-breaking Pro Evo 3, and Nike’s own Apex model, which took the top spot at the NYC marathon and replaces the Alphafly line at the top of the brand’s racing stable.

Still, less experienced runners and those who expect to take four or more hours to finish a marathon might find this to be a bit too much shoe. There are other options that will both be less expensive and friendlier to slower paces. The $280 price puts the Alphafly 4 just $5 more than the comparable Adidas Adios Pro 5 (and it’s actually $5 less at launch than the Alphafly 3). Now that there are more levels of quality for super shoes, rather than just one premier shoe per brand, costs closer to $300 seem to be the norm.

Overall, Nike has done a solid job continuing the Alphafly legacy—there are just way more super-powered racers around now than in the early days of super shoes. Still, the model is going to work for lots of runners. If you’re chasing a goal time and you need something that can be both fast and wearable, the Alphafly 4 is going to be one of your absolute top picks.

Brett Williams, NASM-CPT, PES, a senior editor at Men's Health, is a certified trainer and former pro football player and tech reporter. You can find his work elsewhere at Mashable, Thrillist, and other outlets.

Bitcoin Lender Ledn Moves US Clients Onshore With Newly introduced Custody Accounts

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (659 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, bitcoin lender Ledn is moving beyond loans.
  • Ledn states that spread makes buying bitcoin through its app about half the cost of a standard purchase on the most popular U.S.
  • Recent findings suggest that ledn has lent against bitcoin since 2018 and has serviced more than $11 billion in loans.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, bitcoin lender Ledn is moving beyond loans. The tech giant introduced Ledn Custody on Tuesday, a new account that lets eligible U.S. clients hold bitcoin, gold, stablecoins and U.S. dollars, and buy, sell and swap between them in one place, with no trading fees and a 0.5% spread.

Ledn states that spread makes buying bitcoin through its app about half the cost of a standard purchase on the most popular U.S. bitcoin apps. The launch also moves Ledn’s U.S. clients, previously served from its Cayman Islands entity, to a U.S. tech giant with a U.S. custodian.

Recent findings suggest that ledn has lent against bitcoin since 2018 and has serviced more than $11 billion in loans. Until now, most of its U.S. clients bought their bitcoin elsewhere and moved it to Ledn to borrow against it. The upcoming account brings that first purchase in-house, from buying through to borrowing.

A standard bitcoin purchase on the most popular U.S. apps costs about 0.9% to 1.25% once trading fees and spread are included, according to Ledn’s own analysis of published fees from October. That puts Ledn in direct competition with the trading apps where many Americans buy their first bitcoin.

According to recent reports, on a $1,000 purchase, that works out to about $5 at Ledn against $9 to $12.50 elsewhere. Clients can deposit dollars and hold them in the account, or use them to buy bitcoin, gold and stablecoins. BitGo describes the gold option as tokenized gold.

According to recent reports, “What our clients want is to hold hard assets, whether that’s bitcoin, gold or stablecoins,” Ledn co-founder and Chief Strategy Officer Mauricio Di Bartolomeo said. “Most people buy them in one place, keep them in another, and when they need cash, they sell. Now they can do all three in one account.”.

He added that clients can borrow against their bitcoin instead of selling, “with gold to follow.”.

Recent findings suggest that assets in a Ledn Custody account are held for the benefit of each client by an independent qualified custodian, segregated from Ledn’s own assets and never lent out for interest. BitGo Bank & Trust, a unit of BitGo (BTGO), provides the custody and trading services behind the account.

The custody setup is a selling point for a lender that came through 2022. Ledn states it has returned every client’s collateral across two full market cycles, including the collapse that bankrupted Celsius, BlockFi and Voyager. The organization has also published monthly loan book and proof of reserves data.

According to recent reports, “We’ve spent eight years earning our clients’ trust as a lender,” Ledn co-founder and CEO Adam Reeds said. “If you’re going to be a financial services tech giant, boring is a good thing. We want to be the reliable, stable place where people build their wealth, not a platform with a million features built for trading.”.

The onshore move lines up with Washington’s message. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in May that crypto’s problems stem from “the wild, wild west offshore,” adding, “we got to bring it onshore.” The Clarity Act, the market structure bill he urged Congress to pass, stalled in the Senate in September.

Sources indicate that ledn is chasing a big market. More than 67 million Americans now own crypto, or about one in four U.S. adults, according to a May survey. Competition for bitcoin borrowers is also heating up, with Cross River Bank launching its first bitcoin-backed loans this week.

It has been revealed that ledn has leaned on the capital markets to fund its lending, selling $188 million in bitcoin-backed bonds in February. The custody account now gives the lender a way to win clients before they ever need a loan.

Ledn Custody accounts will roll out to eligible U.S. individual clients over the coming days. The firm prepares to add lending against gold and open more U.S. states in the coming weeks.

Breaking: Is Yeti’s Latest Performance Outdoor Clothing Any Good? I Put It to the Test to Find Out.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1707 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved.
  • In a recent development, IN A SURPRISE move not many saw, Yeti recently rolled out a performance outdoor clothing line.
  • We put three signature garments from the latest five-piece line to test: The Tensleep Hooded Hybrid Jacket, the Tilloo Hooded Rain Jacket, and the Sansaba Fleece 260 Full-Zip.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, IN A SURPRISE move not many saw, Yeti recently rolled out a performance outdoor clothing line. It’s a deviation, sure, but perhaps a sensible one given the brand’s commitment to outdoor gear and all things insulation. As frequent testers of new products in this ever-expanding category, we could not resist the chance to throw them on and put them through the paces in the elements.

We put three signature garments from the latest five-piece line to test: The Tensleep Hooded Hybrid Jacket, the Tilloo Hooded Rain Jacket, and the Sansaba Fleece 260 Full-Zip. For context, the other two pieces are the Caprock Merino Quarter-Zip and the Heuco 310 Full-Zip, essentially siblings of the fleece we tried out. To the brand’s credit, no PFAs are used in the line and all items come with a three-year warranty.

In a recent development, before even testing, there’s plenty to be intrigued by. The pieces show some clear restraint from a brand that tends toward boldness and large logos (you know, like the beloved coolers). You’d barely even know these were Yeti tops, as you really have to hunt for the brand stamp. And there’s a less-is-more approach in the design here, clearly made with active lifestyles and packability in mind (even color-wise, there are only two options max per item, a somewhat refreshing factoid).

Sources indicate that I tried all three pieces over a couple of weeks in the dead of fall in the Pacific Northwest. Translation? They were subjected to downpours, foggy night jogs, chilly mornings, and windy afternoons. I wore them on long walks with the dog, bike commutes in the rain, adventures on muddy trails, and to evening soccer games. I even brought them to the coast during a storm that stirred up high surf and sideways precipitation. Here’s what I think after all the initial testing.

In a recent development, the Tensleep Hooded Hybrid Jacket looks good, there’s no denying as much. The sleek, trim fit works for even the most active functions and we found it never overheated in testing. Lightweight and packable, it’s somewhat nimble thanks to two-way stretch fabric but not as much so as the other two items tested.

The water resistance is also impressive. I walked the dog through a downpour in this jacket for about 30 minutes and came back with just a few moisture spots on my layer beneath. Not bad for a jacket that certainly doesn’t claim to be waterproof (though does sport a water-repellant finish). In drizzle and light rain, you’re just fine in this puffer jacket. In fact, the water would bead up with the same intensity even after many wears, meaning that exterior was done right.

While I liked the felt-lined pockets, I think they could be even warmer. The blend of Expedry Down and traceable European Lavalan Wool insulation is perhaps the jacket’s strongest feature. Going with a hybrid blend affords an ability to tightrope walk that fine-line between breathability and protection from the elements—and the proof was in the performance.

At $400 though, this is not a cheap item by any stretch of the imagination.

It has been revealed that this was my favorite piece of the trio, and arguably the most straightforward. From the superior YKK Aquaguard zipper to the extremely packable nature of the jacket, the Tilloo is a genuine winner. Like a significant boss in your favorite video game, so many jackets in the category have a weak spot hidden somewhere. It usually translates to water seeping in from a cuff or finding its way in through an average zipper. Not here—this jacket is watertight yet breathable.

One of the coolest features is just how quiet this jacket is. As somebody born and raised in the Pacific Northwest, I’ve worn a fair number of waterproof shells. Many of them swish loudly as you move (not unlike Jim Carrey in Dumb and Dumber as he’s pretending to run while driving). This less crinkly option is quite quiet, a bonus you perhaps never knew you desired (but once you have it, it’s hard to go back).

Recent findings suggest that if you’re like me, you like to get outdoors to get away from all the noise. A loud jacket can disrupt an adventure, whether you’re birding in a marsh or scanning for wildlife on a hike. This jacket is not silent but it’s noticeably more hushed than most others, even during animated motions and heavy exercise. The Velcro cuffs create nice clasps over base layers (or just above a smartwatch during a run) while the liner itself is fairly soft to the touch, unlike the less appealing, membrane-like feel you get from so many options. The hood is adjustable and offers a nice panorama without hampering much of your view. And the way it pulls rain off is impressive, meaning you never have to shake off pooling areas like you might with a lesser jacket or umbrella.

It has become my go-to for offseason excursions. While $350 is an undeniable expense, the jacket is worth the price.

In a recent development, straight on, the Sansaba Fleece 260 is incredibly soft (like, you’re gonna want to nuzzle it). The proprietary PrimaLoft Bio Fleece is a sensory joy, with a lovely feel and a density level that seems to hit the Goldilocks spot. Best, it’s a composite of 100% post-consumer recycled materials. These shorter fibers are densely distributed, creating what Yeti classifies as a midweight garment. We’d argue that it performs on the higher end of the spectrum, at least in terms of insulation and warmth. No, it wouldn’t quite cut it on its own for significant stretches in below-freezing conditions, but it does just find in the kind of cold we’re normally subjected to.

In a recent development, the fleece also breathes quite well. I found that it paired nicely with a brisk mountain hike or even a sweaty workout in damp conditions. However, playing under anything more than a light drizzle requires a proper shell to fend off precipitation. We liked the length of the collar, stylish yet still major enough to hide under during chilly gusts of wind.

Billed as a fleece made for movement and strenuous activities, the Sansaba fared pretty well. I really put it to the sword one day, zipping it up for a four-mile run in light rain. Normally, I’d wear a long-sleeve moisture-wicking shirt beneath, but I wanted to see how the fleece would fare atop a regular cotton T-shirt. While it did well at fending off light moisture and pulling some of the sweat from my arms, I was pretty soaked in sweat at the end. A pretty easy fix with a better undershirt, sure, but it indicates that perhaps the fleece can’t quite do the most strenuous activities without an unwanted side effect (props for drying so quickly after the fact, however).

It has been revealed that additional cons? The interior of the pockets could use some work. The plain mesh is boring and doesn’t do much to warm the paws. But the fleece is so warm and welcoming throughout the top that you can just rest your hands elsewhere for a quick warm-up. The collar also hugs the neck nicely. This is bittersweet, as it really cradles the area and keeps it warm; however, if you like to duck your chin and mouth (and a little nose) beneath this part of a top during a wind gust, it’s harder to do as it’s fairly snug. For $180, this is a pretty good deal, but not necessarily superior to several other fleeces at a similar price point.

Industry observers note that while you don’t need the whole set, you might want a few of these pieces to bolster your outdoor apparel game. I recommend them all, but with some caveats. The rain jacket is the best item for the price and is very much on par with others in the category.

The puffer is nice but I don’t find it a whole lot better than, say, this one from Wren that I’ve been wearing for a couple of years now (the Columbia Terwilliger Treail Heat Seal Jacket is another fine option). The neat, textured, and non-glossy (per so, so many) look is hard to beat, but it’s a significant chunk of change even give its merits.

The fleece is also an attractive piece of outerwear with some high-performance capabilities, but perhaps not at the same level as some of its counterparts at its decidedly high price point. I tends toward options like the Patagonia Better Jacket and the Trailmade from REI, a bargain-and-a-half. But the Sansaba is an undoubtedly good-looking option with a lot going for it.

Yeti is clearly on to something here and has turned heads with a combination of clean fits, useful tech, and designs with mobility in mind (not to mention some environmentally conscious moves too). But this writer would suggest splurging on perhaps just one of the items depending on your adventuring angles and lifestyle.

Industry observers note that real talk: Deodorant isn't a sexy beauty product, but it's arguably one of the most important. Imagine plopping down on your exercise bike, pounding the pavement in your favorite running gear, or even just commuting to the office without one. Scary thought, right? Growing up in notoriously humid South Florida, I was always hyper-aware of body odor and well-acquainted with underarm sweat—and I knew that deodorant was the way to keep me dry and stink-free.

According to recent reports, I've no doubt that one of the products below will get the job done beautifully for you (so please, scroll!). But here are a few expert pointers if you want to shop for the best deodorant on your own.

It has been revealed that "Keeping underarms fresh involves two main goals: controlling sweat and eliminating B.O.," says dermatologist Blair Murphy-Rose, MD. That's where deodorants and antiperspirants come into play. The only problem? People often use the terms interchangeably, but they're actually very different.

Deodorants help mask or neutralize underarm odor caused by sweat mixing with skin bacteria, while antiperspirants use aluminum to reduce underarm sweat by blocking sweat glands, notes Dr. Murphy-Rose. "One potential downside with antiperspirants is that they can dry out surrounding skin, leading to irritation, itching, and rash for those with sensitive skin," adds Alicia Zalka, MD, a dermatologist and associate clinical professor at Yale University School of Medicine.

According to recent reports, controlling sweat and masking bad odors are both key, but you'll have to be honest to decide which is a higher priority for your needs. If you're a heavy sweater and want to stop underarm wetness, opt for antiperspirants. If excess perspiration isn't as big of an concern for you, stick with deodorants. My daily go-to is deodorant, but I swiped both types to share the full scoop on the best women's deodorants and antiperspirants in the game. And the best part? Everything starts at just $9.

Industry observers note that you've probably seen a variety of deodorant and antiperspirant formulations, and Dr. Murphy-Rose states your choice should be based upon personal preference and your unique issues. That said, there are some differences between the different types, so here's a quick rundown to think about.

Sources indicate that solids and sticks typically have a waxy consistency, are generally well-tolerated, and usually are the best for sensitive skin. Dragging on the skin is usually the primary source of irritation with these, so "try warming the stick on your skin first before swiping to minimize friction," advises Dr. Murphy-Rose. They also tend to leave behind annoying powdery white streaks on dark clothes and stickiness on the underarm area, adds Dr. Zalka. (All of these featured solids and sticks did not leave behind any residue on my clothes.).

Recent findings suggest that gels are convenient roll-ons and are typically light or clear so naturally, they leave behind less residue than solids. The only downside is that they tend to feel wet on skin—so if you're already dealing with excess perspiration, you may not love that sensation.

It has been revealed that creams feel moisturizing and soothing with application, but are a bit more messy and not as easy to apply. They're totally worth using, especially if you're looking to concentrate the application to a specific area or want full-body coverage (think between skin folds or under your breasts). Creams are typically more hydrating than gels and are a good option for those prone to dryness or irritation, notes Dr. Murphy-Rose.

Sources indicate that spray deodorants are quick to use, lightweight, and typically fast-drying, so they're practical for days you're in a rush. "They feel light and dry quickly with fewer ingredients," indicates Dr. Zalka. However, some may contain alcohol, which can be dehydrating or irritating for sensitive skin. Sprays can also be messy because you can't fully control where all of the deodorant particles land.

Sources indicate that in general, you'll want to use deodorants made with moisturizing ingredients like humectants like hyaluronic acid or glycerin for hydration and occlusives like shea butter or beeswax to help protect dry, itchy underarms, recommends board-certified dermatologist Hadley King, MD. There are also deodorants made with bentonite clay, powders, or baking soda to help combat moisture. Crucial to note: "None of these ingredients blocks sweat ducts—they work by absorbing moisture," she says. Dr. Murphy-Rose is also keen on deodorants made with low concentrations of alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs) to minimize underarm discoloration and baking soda.

That's slightly different from antiperspirants, which use aluminum salts to stop perspiration by creating plugs that block sweat glands, using aluminum, says Dr. Murphy-Rose. She adds that most over-the-counter antiperspirants contain 12 to 25 percent aluminum, while prescription-strength formulas can go up to about 30 percent.

I'm our resident scent-obsessed beauty editor and have tried a slew of deodorants and antiperspirants throughout my nearly decade-long journalism career. For this story, I kept the above dermatologist-approved guidance in mind and carefully researched hundreds of women's deodorants and antiperspirants.

Industry observers note that next, I went to the Women's Health beauty closet and revisited products in my personal collection until I eventually narrowed down my list to 24 potential contenders that seemed promising. I tested these deodorants after showering and, on weekends spent indoors, I delayed showering my underarms to see how these products held up against smell and sweat. I also considered how much odor and sweat protection they provide while exercising, running errands across New York City, and wearing them on special occasions and nights out with friends.

I also considered their ease of use, how they feel on my underarms, whether they leave behind any residue (a major pet peeve of mine), and how frequently I needed to apply to remain confident in how I smell.

With that, I give you: the best women's deodorants of 2026. They are all loved by me, and some are even well-known among the dermatologists I spoke with for this story. Regardless of which deodorant you order, they all earned major snaps from me, a very hard-to-please beauty editor. The best part? They all start at just $9 and don’t leave behind embarrassing white marks on clothing. Sign me up for bulk orders!

Zendaya and Tom Holland may have tied the knot, but they’re still marking latest milestones together. The actors have reportedly purchased their first piece of real estate together. The Daily Mail broke the news, alleging that the Spider-Man co-stars paid about $10.8 million (£8.25 million) cash for a five-bedroom house in an undisclosed London suburb described as “exclusive” and “leafy.”.

According to recent reports, there are few publicly known facts about the property—which isn’t much of a surprise, considering it took months for the notably private couple to confirm that they had gotten married. While AD could not independently confirm the purchase, reports say that the stars scored a sizable discount on the property, which was listed with a price tag of $11.8 million (£9 million).

Per the Daily Mail’s reporting, the 5,000-square-foot dwelling sits on a one-acre plot and features four bathrooms and four reception rooms. “My youngest is very excited that Spider-Man is going to be living across the street,” an inhabitant of a neighboring home told the Daily Mail. “I told him, ‘You will have to kick a ball a long way to reach their back garden.’ I doubt they will have a housewarming party.”.

Since 2018, Holland has owned a six-bedroom home in Kingston-upon-Thames in southwest London. He paid $3.35 million (£2.5 million) for the six-bedroom residence, which he extensively renovated from 2020 until 2023, when Zendaya reportedly moved in. The Dune star maintains several properties stateside: a $1.4 million five-bedroom, five-bathroom Mediterranean-style house near Los Angeles; a 5,000-square-foot, ranch-style home in Encino, California, for which she paid $3.97 million; and a $4.9 million three-bedroom condo in Brooklyn’s luxe Quay Tower.

Sources indicate that the Hollywood pair is likely to remain tight-lipped about their alleged newly introduced property, since privacy has been an issue for them in the past. Last year, it was reported that they were spending $1,300 a day on security for their Kingston-upon-Thames dwelling after fans started gathering at the front gates.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that WINTER IS SWIFTLY approaching. But whether you’re a front-country weekend warrior or a hardcore backcountry camper, you still should have a few camping trips lined up for the year (leaf-peeping fall road trip, anyone?). And it’s never too late to take stock of your gear closet to see what’s missing, what’s busted, and what needs an upgrade.

We cover all the latest and greatest outdoor gear every year in the Men’s Health Outdoor Awards. But, in this guide, we’re covering just the greatest. To offer a wide breadth of options (since there are all different sorts of camping), we’ve broken this guide into categories of tents, sleep systems, kitchen, and general camping gear. Whether it’s all new for 2026 or it’s been around for years, these are our favorite camping and outdoor gear picks for backpacking, car camping, and everything in between—the gear that we love and pack for every trip.

This entry-level tent strikes a good balance of pack weight, affordability, and reliability. It’s roomy enough to sleep two with a dash of gear and sets up faster than most at this price point (even with the included rainfly) for easy-breezy camping in almost any season. Bonus: A limited lifetime warranty.

Read More: Best Hiking Boots for Men.

Nemo’s Aurora 3 ticks all our must-have boxes for a midrange, midsize tent. It sleeps three (tightly) or two who appreciate spreading out with more gear. A generously sized interior, plus oversized doors and vestibules, provides a much more livable space. We love that the hubbed pole design makes for a dead-simple setup and teardown. Plus, Nemo’s commitment to more eco-friendly gear means a bluesign-approved recycled tent floor and PFAS-free rainfly.

Read More: Do I Need Trekking Poles?

Industry observers note that redesigned for 2026, Sea to Summit upgrades its already fantastic Telos Evo tent line to be even more livable and weatherproof. A dedicated roof vent (with storm flap) promotes better airflow and reduces condensation. The versatile design also offers multiple pitch options, including hangout and stargaze modes. So it’s not only a reliable backcountry sleep space, but a day/night lounge when you need it.

The Lunar Solo is a budgversatility for extra gear or your dog. Plus, it’s durable and breathable with solid ventilation. It’s not the single best in any one category, but the price makes it a great all-arounder for weight-conscious backpackers and thru-hikers on a budget. Our main gripes are the tricky setup process and the fact that it requires seam sealing before use—neither of which is a deal breaker at this price point though.

In a recent development, marmot sought to reinvent the wheel, er, sleeping bag with its all-upcoming Wraptor. The clever design swaps traditional zippers for overlapping flips and magnetic snaps, ensuring a more versatile camp sleep setup. Shed the layers in warmer weather or bundle up when the temperature drops—it’s flexible in every temperature. This same adjustability caters to sleepers who appreciate a “swaddled like a baby” mummy bag and hybrid campers looking for more room to spread out on their stomachs and sides. Also available in a 15-degree option.

Read More: Marmot Wraptor Review.

According to recent reports, exped’s midrange Terra line is our go-to bag for anyone looking for real, 650-fill-power duck down that’s affordable. The 15-degree temp rating makes this a solid three-season option that’s capable of most four-season camping in all but the coldest weather. It’s comfy enough for car camping, and with a roughly 3-pound pack weight, compact enough for backpacking overnighters. The glow-in-the-dark zipper pull and internal pocket are nifty features, too.

Read More: The Best Car Camping Gear.

Sources indicate that with the Cot One, Helinox creates an instant sleep surface that’s flat, level, comfortable, and off the ground. Fully set up, it’s the perfect front-country camp bed that supports more than 300 pounds. It packs down surprisingly small into the included zip case and weighs less than five pounds. Optional leg extensions are available to lift the cot up to 15 inches off the ground for maximum comfort.

Sources indicate that this entry-level model from Wise Owl Outfitters is a great starter option for anyone looking to get into hammock camping or as a budget-friendly “just in case” hammock. The lightweight design weighs less than two pounds for the hammock, straps, carabiners, and stuff sack. It’s surprisingly durable and supports up to 500 pounds. Bonus: It’s available in more than a dozen colors, too.

It has been revealed that you typically get what you pay for in the world of inflatable air pads, but Klymit’s Static V Base is something of a unicorn. It’s plenty comfy for front-country camp setups, but it really shines in the backcountry with a compact, featherweight construction that’s surprisingly durable to survive rock punctures and uneven ground. Most impressive? It’s typically available for less than $50.

In a recent development, we’ll take a proper foam pillow over an inflatable any day. Therm-a-Rest’s fan-favorite compressible relies on an upcycled foam fill and a plush polyester cover for serious front- and backcountry sleep comfort that’s the closest thing to your home bedroom setup. The cinch adjuster (hence the name) allows campers to tweak the pillow’s firmness to their liking. Plus, it packs down to about half its size for easy travel.

In a recent development, for front-country campers with access to electricity (or even a portable power station), Nestout’s Outdoor Cooker adds serious versatility to your outdoor kitchen. The modest 500-watt capability is plenty powerful for cooking rice, boiling, steaming, or whipping up everything from soup to oatmeal. At less than two pounds, it’s compact and lightweight enough to stash in the back of your rig until you need it.

Yeti’s newest cast-iron skillet is also the largest in its lineup. The 14-inch size makes it ideal as an all-in-one pan for car campers looking to pack less cookware. The oversized design comes polished and pre-seasoned, so it’s ready to go right out of the box. An additional grab handle and dual pour spouts make it safer and ultra-versatile for cooking up just about anything.

In a recent development, this portable fridge from BougeRV is the perfect accompaniment to your existing cooler. Stash the temperature critical foods (meat, eggs, bacon, etc.) in the former and everything else in the latter. It’s small enough to fit in the footwell of most passenger vehicles, and the included 240Wh detachable battery keeps it cold for more than a full day. What’s more: It’s more affordable than most premium midsize coolers.

Industry observers note that gerber elevates the lowly spork with the ComplEAT Multi-Fork. It’s the same multipurpose utensil we all know and love, including a deep-basin spoon, a tined fork end, and dual cut/scrape edges. But this premium take adds a six-function multi-tool that clips to the back. So, you also get a serrated package opener, a can opener, a bottle opener, twin flathead drivers, and a pry bar. A clever kickstand feature also keeps the business end up off of dirty rocks and ground.

For campers who value weight and packability above all else, BioLite’s CampStove 2+ is a game-changer. The clever design runs on pretty much any organic material (twigs, pine cones, leaves, wood) to keep it stoked off-grid almost indefinitely. The dual-purpose output charges your phone, GPS, headlamp, and other small devices (at up to three watts) in the backcountry, and it doubles as a stove at mealtime.

I’m willing to dump a lot of things from my pack to save weight, but coffee isn’t one of them. Sea to Summit’s Frontier Ultralight Collapsible Pour Over is as dead-simple and packable as a camp coffeemaker can get, so you’re guaranteed your morning Joe anywhere. It weighs just two ounces and folds down almost completely flat so you’ll practically forget it’s in your backpack. But it pops open to reveal a legit pour-over coffeemaker that works with most camp and travel mugs.

In a recent development, for serious front-country campers, Jetboil’s Genesis Basecamp is near perfect. The dual-burner system allows for more elaborate meal preparation than single-burner alternatives with up to 10,000 BTU output and maximum flame control. A 5-liter pot and 10-inch ceramic-coated nonstick fry pan are included, so you can prep just about anything for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, even for larger groups.

The all-latest Daytrip 20L combines Yeti’s legendary all-day, keep-cold insulation with the portability of a traditional backpack cooler. It’s roomy enough for a six-pack, two lunches, snacks, and an ice pack, making it perfect for day-hike lunch breaks or even as add-on cold storage for weekend trips. A large top opening provides easy access, while external pockets add extra storage for keeping smaller essentials within easy reach.

For long weekends at the campsite or off-grid, we love this oversized cooler from RTIC. The 78-can capacity offers plenty of cold storage for a family getaway, and RTIC’s premium insulation ensures it stays chilled for up to five days. The lightweight design is easier to carry, and all-terrain, puncture-proof wheels make it easy to wheel from the car to the campsite, too.

Sources indicate that car camping is dirty business—literally. That’s why we love simple, versatile adventure storage that just works. Upgrade your existing loadout with this gear box from Gregory. It’s waterproof/dustproof, and the translucent lid makes organization infinitely easier than with traditional opaque storage totes. Plus, the clever hinged lid opens either way for easy access.

Sources indicate that solo Stove has long been a perennial favorite for us here at Men’s Health. Its latest Basecamp fire pit combines a just-right size that’s roomy enough for four adults to enjoy yet compact enough to easily transport from the backyard to the backseat for car camping. And, of course, it still features the same smokeless design and maximum burn efficiency that the brand is known for.

Recent findings suggest that leatherman’s Signal has been my multitool of choice since I can remember. The just-right tool selection includes everything you need for a day in the backcountry or your own backyard: Pliers, drivers, cutters, a saw, a micro hammer, bottle and can openers, wrenches, and a 420 HC combo knife. Plus, there’s a whistle and ferro rod if you need ‘em. It’s all packed into one compact tool that stuffs neatly in the available sheath or clips to your pack with the brand that invented the ultra-packable camp chair sought to make it even better. With an extended backrest, it’s now more comfortable and supportive than ever, with all the same backpacking-friendly packability as before. The shock-corded pole structure makes for easy setup, and the 100% recycled polyester seat fabric is a nice, eco-friendly touch.

It has been revealed that the brand that invented the ultra-packable camp chair sought to make it even better. With an extended backrest, it’s now more comfortable and supportive than ever, with all the same backpacking-friendly packability as before. The shock-corded pole structure makes for easy setup, and the 100% recycled polyester seat fabric is a nice, eco-friendly touch.

The aptly named GigaPower Folding Torch is the single best way to start a campfire in any conditions. It uses the same small disposable fuel canisters that you’re probably already packing. Yet it’s powerful enough for starting large fires while car camping and compact enough to stash in a backpack if you’re planning to backcountry camp. Plus, it’s just so damn fun to use.

In a recent development, our go-to camp table balances weight and durability, with a dead-simple design that makes setup and breakdown easy. The nearly flat silhouette slots neatly into the laptop sleeve of a backpack or soft cooler, too.

According to recent reports, bluetti’s Elite 100 V2 is the portable power station to buy if you only want to buy one. It’s relatively lightweight and compact enough to stash in the footwell of most vehicles. But the 1800-watt peak output can power everything from smartphones and laptops to rice cookers and blenders. It’s surprisingly affordable, too, especially compared to the competition. Just add a 100-watt folding solar panel for virtually limitless off-grid power.

Simple touches can elevate any car camping setup. Rumpl’s aptly named Everywhere Mat combines a great-looking microsuede topside that’s stain- and water-resistant with a durable waterproof bottom. So, you get the added livability of a true outdoor rug, including a softer place to walk and for your kids/pets to rest, and a way to protect your gear from stains, wet ground, and errant sticks and rocks.

In a recent development, another solid storage option, Thule’s upcoming Chasm 55L (and Chasm 80L) is plenty durable for outdoor use, with a molded EVA waterproof base. The semi-rigid structure stays upright when you need it, and the included movable panel lets you customize the interior layout to fit your setup. A zippered lid cleverly folds open and secures magnetically, so you can use it in either the full-open or half-open position.

It has been revealed that while Black Diamond’s Spot 400-R is a bit of a gold standard when it comes to headlamps, you might need something a little stronger in certain outdoor situations. In comes the new Storm Headlamp, which can generate 550 lumens up to a distance of 137 meters. It also incorporates RGB lighting options and offers rechargeability via USB-C. While the 70 hours of runtime on low (4 on high and 30 on medium) is a tad short, this headlamp is going to go anywhere and do anything you need it to.

Sources indicate that there is no one way to camp, especially these days. Here’s a quick rundown on the different camping styles.

Sources indicate that the key isn't just packing more gear, but packing high-quality items that are durable, versatile, and work for your style of camping. That last bit is the most vital. Focus on the things that actually make your experience better. For me, that means an ultra-comfortable sleep setup (with a luxurious portable mattress and a legit camp pillow) that's almost as good as my bed at home, and a solid camp kitchen (with a portable fridge and premium cookware set) because I love to cook. But that changes from the frontcountry to the backcountry.

Sources indicate that depending on how remote you’re going, you should figure out your own preferences for your style of camping. Weight savings is always more crucial when you step up from car camping and into more involved situations in the backcountry.

Recent findings suggest that weather and climate are always a factor when camping. Not just for what to pack and bring, but for the type of gear you invest in. Are you just a summer camper? Then you can probably get away with three-season camping gear. If you do want to do winter camping, then having two sets of gear (one for warmer and one for colder) might make sense or opting for four-season gear might be the way to go.

In a recent development, there are solo campers all the way to massive group camping excursions, and everything in between. Making sure you have the right size tent for the people you tend to camp with is a first start. Maybe you like solo camping often, but you do a group trip every summer as well. You’ll probably need two tents then, or at least making sure that someone in the group has more of a three-person and up tent. The same thinking should go into your camp kitchen setup.

Recent findings suggest that as an avid camper and adventure travel writer for more than two decades, I've tested countless outdoor products from all of the world's most recognized brands. Whether that’s a weeklong car camping trip or backpacking throughout Utah’s national parks, I’ve assessed outdoor gear in countless different scenarios and climates. I also consulted with Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower on top options, research, and some of his own personal testing.

While testing camping gear, we've been sure to take thorough notes on comfort, ease of packing, weight, durability, functionality, performance, and necessity. The best camping gear is the gear you actually use, as overpacking can make things a bit tricky. Prioritize what’s best for your style of camping.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • Sources indicate that from sweaty runs and heat styling to product buildup, our scalps and hair need proper TLC—and that starts with a great shampoo.
  • In a recent development, “I always tell my clients that shampoo is mainly for your scalp, so I would start there,” notes trichologist and hairstylist Courtney Foster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that from sweaty runs and heat styling to product buildup, our scalps and hair need proper TLC—and that starts with a great shampoo. Our scalp is an extension of the skin on our face—it sheds dead skin cells, collects dirt and bacteria, and secretes oil and sweat, says trichologist Anabel Kingsley in our guide on how often to shampoo your hair. While the beauty community has mixed opinions on the cadence of shampooing, dermatologist DiAnne Davis, MD, recommends doing so at least once a week. The frequency varies based on your lifestyle, how promptly your hair gets greasy, your scalp health, and hair type. Since the experts advise regular shampooing, I asked the pros about how we can upgrade our healthy hair routines to preserve the expensive chemical and color treatments we enjoy at the salon.

In a recent development, “I always tell my clients that shampoo is mainly for your scalp, so I would start there,” notes trichologist and hairstylist Courtney Foster. “You can have curly hair with an oily scalp, fine hair with a dry scalp, or color-treated hair with buildup. Hair type matters, but it doesn't tell me everything I need to know.” Choose hydrating shampoos that nourish a dry scalp, or use a lightweight shampoo with fewer moisturizing ingredients for an oily scalp.

For an oily scalp or buildup, ingredients like salicylic acid can be helpful, along with gentle cleansing agents like coco glucoside. For mineral and hard water buildup, look for chelating ingredients, as regular shampoo alone may not remove these deposits, according to Foster.

Now it’s time to think about your hair type, advises Foster. In addition to your hair texture, you’ll want to find a shampoo that’s suitable for your dry, chemically treated, damaged, or breakage-prone mane.

For dryness, humectants and conditioning ingredients such as glycerin, hyaluronic acid, and nourishing oils are your new beauty best friends. They help the hair retain moisture and feel softer and more manageable, says Foster.

For damaged hair, you’ll need shampoos packed with amino acids and bond-strengthening ingredients. “These are good for hair that has been chemically treated or excessively heat-styled,” she says of components such as hydrolyzed proteins, which can improve the feel and strength of damaged hair.

According to recent reports, now, if you’re dealing with frizz like I am, it likely means the hair is lacking moisture, says Foster. We’ll benefit from conditioning ingredients like polymers, silicones, oils, and humectants that help smooth the cuticle and improve manageability.

As our hair-obsessed beauty editor, I own a sizable shampoo collection. It’s 24 shampoos strong. So I started there and narrowed it down to 12 contenders. The Kids Are Outside: The Rise of the Adult Children’s ADU

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Diane and Steve Weaver of Castro Valley, California, shipped their son Sam off to college in 2013, they hoped he’d someday find his dream job and a nice home.
  • While in-law suites and granny flats (a nickname for when ADUs house in-laws) have become popular among young, successful homeowners who want their elderly parents nearby, a growing number of Americans are now adding ADUs to their properties to house adult children threatening to move back in and reverse their status as empty nesters.
  • According to recent reports, blame the return of the flock on the home affordability crisis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Diane and Steve Weaver of Castro Valley, California, shipped their son Sam off to college in 2013, they hoped he’d someday find his dream job and a nice home. And while Sam is thriving professionally as a sales rep with his own place, they never expected that his house would be in their backyard. But the nightmarish Bay Area real estate market made a 400-square-foot ADU (accessory dwelling unit) on his parents’ property, complete with a separate entrance and direct street access, seem like the best option for the 32-year-old. “It was becoming difficult for him to afford rent while also saving toward eventually buying a place of his own,” Diane tells AD. “He’s close by, but it really feels like he has his own home.”.

While in-law suites and granny flats (a nickname for when ADUs house in-laws) have become popular among young, successful homeowners who want their elderly parents nearby, a growing number of Americans are now adding ADUs to their properties to house adult children threatening to move back in and reverse their status as empty nesters.

Diane and Steve Weaver on their property’s ADU.

According to recent reports, blame the return of the flock on the home affordability crisis. These days a homebuyer needs an annual income between $110,000 and $113,000—well above the national average income of $64,220 per year—to comfortably afford a median-priced home in the US, which is presently priced at $434,900. While this has led some grown kids to move back into their childhood bedrooms, in cases where acreage allows, families like the Weavers are opting to be neighbors instead of housemates by setting up self-contained living spaces on the same lot as their single-family homes. In California, they’re certainly no outlier. The state has passed legislation specifically encouraging the construction of ADUs to address the housing shortage—which resulted in quadruple the number of ADU permits issued in the Golden State from 2017 to 2022.

Industry observers note that those in the ADU construction game say families like the Weavers make up an increasingly large slice of their business. Jeremy Nova, co-founder of the Colorado-based prefab ADU builder Studio Home, says ADUs for adult children are popular among his clients because the arrangement is mutually beneficial. The kids are afforded some independence and the ability to save money, “while for the parents, it can also be a long-term investment. The same space that houses an adult child today could eventually become a rental or a separate living space for a caregiver.” ADU builders on the opposite coast are seeing the same demand. Justin Olewack, president of Bolt Builders, says that ADUs for adult children are becoming a top request among his clientele in the DC, Virginia, and Maryland areas, where housing costs have risen 61 percent since 2016.

If it cuts costs and results in a sellable amenity down the line, perhaps moving back home isn’t the failure-to-launch scenario it was once seen as.

An ADU by Studio Home, built in the backyard of a Scottsdale, Arizona, family’s property.

In a recent development, once a family’s adult child moves out of the property’s ADU, especially if it has a kitchen and bathroom, the structure can serve as a rental, providing passive income for retired parents. Tracy Noh, who hired John Brennan of BZBuild Co to build her daughter Eliza Bowen an ADU in Burbank, was thinking long-term with her compound planning. “An in-home apartment would require sharing the space of our 1,000-square-foot main home. And, as someone who works from home, the ADU seemed a better solution,” she indicates.

Noh and Eliza show off their Burbank ADU.

The living arrangement has also enabled Noh and her daughter to develop their own life paths. The structure gives her daughter a space in which she can become a young adult, and Noh the opportunity to step back from making the day-to-day household decisions. The former is learning how to manage her own household: planning meals, budgeting expenses, and making time for household chores.

Recent findings suggest that “That change in dynamic also allows us both to remain much calmer in our interactions with each other,” Noh claims. It’s not just because there’s a separate place for each of them to retreat to; Noh says she has “gained an enormous amount of respect for Eliza and her ability to manage her own home. It’s a fabulous opportunity to begin to build that adult-to-adult relationship with your child.”.

The interior of Tracy Noh’s ADU by BZBuild Co.

While modest ADUs serve single occupants just fine, more sizable ADUs allow a family’s adult children to bring their own kids in tow. Oren Amir, co-founder of SoCal builder GO Home Builders, points out that in his experience, the catalyst for aging parents to build an ADU for their adult children is almost never just the adult child themselves: It’s the grandchild they will be bringing with them. “The call comes a few months before or after a baby arrives,” he notes. The grandparents don’t want to travel to visit their grandkids; they want them living nearby. Rent in Los Angeles is what stops people from saving, and early parenthood is when saving matters most, Amir says. An ADU in a grandparent’s backyard, therefore, lets the adult children stay in the neighborhood, raise the baby near help, and set some money aside for when the time comes to leave the nest for good. “Everyone gets what they need and nobody has to move in,” Amir says of the arrangement.

It has been revealed that while the Weaver family ADU is Sam’s for now, it could grow up to be a granny flat someday. “It’s possible that Sam might live in the main house and we could move into the ADU as we age,” says Diane. “It gives us a lot of options for how the space can be used as our family’s needs change.”.

The second season of their show Nelly & Ashanti: We Belong Together is streaming now on Peacock, and follows the couple as they juggle married life, hectic careers, and raising their toddler son Kareem Kenkaide (aka “KK”). Through all of their highs and lows, they have each other’s back—and display insane chemistry while doing so.

Women’s Health recently got a glimpse of their playful dynamic when the couple stopped by for a round of “In Fitness and In Health,” the game that puts their knowledge of each other to the test. Given that Nelly and Ashanti first met all the way back in the early 2000s (they dated for 10 years before breaking up in 2013, only to rekindle things in 2023), they pretty much passed with flying colors.

Yes, Nelly knows his bride well, even if he’s still learning the correct definition of “love language.”.

“Your love language...English?” he guesses, making Ashanti laugh before changing his answer: “Birkin?”.

“I'll take Birkin!” Ashanti says with a grin. “Thank you! One coming on the way.”.

When the question turns to Nelly’s secret talent, Ashanti has an answer at the ready: “I don't know if it's too much of a secret, but you are a really good athlete,” she says. “You play baseball very well; football very well. And you hoop.”.

“That’s right,” Nelly states proudly.

Recent findings suggest that and he’s not the only athlete in the family. When Nelly is asked which Olympic sport Ashanti would partake in, he confidently answers “track.” And he’s right on the money.

“I was actually scouted by the Olympics when I was in high school,” Ashanti indicates. “I used to do the triple jump, and I made the Wall of Fame at my school.”.

Recent findings suggest that maybe the couple’s next show should be titled Karaoke Relay, and instead of passing a baton, they pass the mic! (You can have that idea for free, guys!) Either way, it’s clear these two dynamos really do belong together.

The 15 Best Jeans for Men, Tested and Reviewed by Style Editors

📅 22 Aug 2023 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4712 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
