The 10 Best Fitness Trackers for Women, Tested and Reviewed by Editors

📅 06 Nov 2018 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3911 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • Sources indicate that finding the right fitness tracker is less about buying the most advanced wearable out there and more about choosing the one that will actually work for how you’ll use it to help you meet your fitness goals.
  • For this guide, we considered a range of fitness trackers for different training styles and tracking needs, from simple bands for everyday activity tracking to running watches, smartwatches, screenless wearables, and smart rings, all designed to monitor sleep, recovery, fitness, and health trends over time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that finding the right fitness tracker is less about buying the most advanced wearable out there and more about choosing the one that will actually work for how you’ll use it to help you meet your fitness goals. You may want a smartwatch that can handle calls and texts along with fitness data tracking, or maybe you’re looking for a distraction-free screenless band that quietly tracks your metrics in the background. If running is your thing, you may want a smartwatch with GPS accuracy and real-time training metrics that are easy to read during a run, and if you’re focused on improving sleep, you may prefer a smart ring that won’t feel bulky overnight.

For this guide, we considered a range of fitness trackers for different training styles and tracking needs, from simple bands for everyday activity tracking to running watches, smartwatches, screenless wearables, and smart rings, all designed to monitor sleep, recovery, fitness, and health trends over time.

Whoop earned the top spot for the best overall fitness tracker because it provides deeper understanding of your data while also giving context of what all that data means. I’ve been using a Whoop for the past several years, and of all the fitness tracker options I’ve tested, it remains my hands-down favorite. It delivers some of the most useful recovery, sleep, and strain insights in a distraction-free design that’s so comfortable I often completely forget that I’m wearing it. The battery life is impressive, and I only have to charge mine twice a month.

Whoop 5.0 is built on the foundation of an app that offers analysis of your metrics paired with context, so you actually learn what all the numbers mean for your health and training. The screen-free design means that instead of buzzing constantly or encouraging you to check another display, it quietly tracks your metrics in the background and turns that data into recovery, strain, sleep data to give you an overall picture of your fitness within an app.

The sensor platform uses multi-wavelength optical heart rate sensors, skin-temperature sensing, blood oxygen monitoring, and accelerometer and gyroscope motion sensors to collect data continuously, tracking your resting heart rate, heart rate variability, respiratory rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, sleep stages, strain, and recovery.

The app then interprets those numbers, in a way that feels more actionable than raw data alone, to generate a daily readiness score that indicates how much physical exertion your body is up for on any given day (00033though it’s always crucial to listen to your body regardless of what a wearable indicates). If you wake up with a low recovery score, for example, Whoop may recommend reducing workout intensity. If your sleep debt is climbing, it will show how much rest you need to get back on track.

It also offers other behavior change suggestions that could improve how you feel based on the data it collects about you and your habits over time. In fact, the in-depth habit tracking feature offers some of the most valuable insights into how day-to-day behaviors affect us physiologically. As a trainer, this has been one of the features I've seen make the most long-term impact with clients, as it really helps them connect the dots and understand how everything is interrelated.

Whoop 5.0 does require a membership and there are three different tiers, the main difference being the level of insights and analysis. Whoop One covers the core Whoop experience, including sleep, strain, recovery, steps, activity monitoring, heart-rate tracking, and women’s hormonal insights, which helps us see how menstrual cycle phases may relate to sleep, recovery, and performance. Whoop Peak adds a broader health and wellness layer, including health monitor, stress monitor, healthspan, and more advanced coaching-style insights for users who want to connect daily habits with longer-term performance and recovery trends (this is the tier I personally go with). Whoop Life is the most advanced tier, adding heart-health features such as ECG, irregular heart rhythm notifications, and blood pressure insights where available. Ultimately, the difference between the tiers is less about the tracker experience itself and more about how much interpretation, health context, and advanced monitoring you want.

In a recent development, the tradeoff is cost. Since Whoop uses a membership model, it will end up being more expensive over time than a tracker that doesn’t require a subscription. It also is not the best choice if you want live pace, distance, or workout stats on your wrist during a run. For that, a Garmin, Apple Watch, Samsung Galaxy Watch, or COROS watch will be more practical.

The Google Fitbit Inspire earned its spot as the best budget pick because it gives you the core fitness-tracking features most people want in a slim and approachable design. It’s not trying to be a full smartwatch or a performance running watch. Instead, it focuses on the basics: steps, heart rate, workouts, sleep, active minutes, and general wellness trends.

In a recent development, that simplicity makes the Fitbit Inspire a good entry point for someone who wants to become more aware of their fitness data without getting buried in advanced metrics. It can track walks, gym workouts, casual runs, and sleep, while the Fitbit app makes the data easy to understand. You can quickly see how much movement you got throughout the day, how long you slept, and how your habits are trending over time. Additionally, you’ll get a stress management score, guided breathing sessions, and reminders to move.

It is also one of the easiest trackers to wear all day. The band is slim enough to feel less bulky than a smartwatch, and the display is small but still easy to use for checking basic stats. If your main goals are walking more, staying accountable, improving sleep habits, or getting started with activity tracking, the Inspire offers strong value.

The main limitation is that it’s not necessarily built for serious training. Depending on the model, the GPS may rely on your phone rather than being fully built into the device, and runners who want advanced pace analysis, training load, recovery guidance, or race tools will likely outgrow it. But for the price, it’s one of the most practical fitness trackers for everyday use.

It has been revealed that the Apple Watch Series 12 blends health tracking, workout features, smartwatch convenience, and safety tools better than almost any other wearable. If you already use an iPhone, this is the most seamless option in our guide.

Sources indicate that the Series 12 features more advanced sensor capabilities, including an upgraded optical heart sensor that measures heart rate every five seconds, and tracks HRV more frequently. WH associate fitness editor Addison Aloin wrote in her review that the Series 12 has “a great baseline of health and fitness features.”.

The Series 12 tracks a wide range of workouts, including running, walking, cycling, strength training, HIIT, yoga, Pilates, swimming, hiking, and many more. During activity, the display is bright and you can easily view data like pace, distance, heart rate, time, and workout zones during runs and workouts. It also integrates smoothly with Apple Fitness+, the Health app, and third-party training apps.

One of the most meaningful updates the Series 12 got is a latest readiness score, which uses recent activity, training load, your sleep score, and overnight metrics like heart rate, respiratory rate, skin temperature, and recovery HRV to estimate how prepared your body is for exertion. The score runs from 0 to 10 and gives you a recommendation for your day, such as Recover, Pace Yourself, Ready, or Go For It. “My only complaint is that it’s kind of hard to find the readiness score on the watch and in the Health app,” Aloin states.

It has been revealed that since it’s so much more than just a tracker you wear during workout, the Apple Watch also offers a lot of versatility. It can handle notifications, calls, music, maps, timers, contactless payments, fall detection, and emergency features, making it a strong option for anyone who wants one device that can move between workouts and everyday life.

It has been revealed that it is also a good pick for people who like motivational nudges. Apple’s activity rings are simple, visual, and surprisingly effective if you respond well to daily goals. If you want coaching-style feedback without digging through complex training dashboards, the Series 12’s newer software can translate health and fitness data into easily digestible prompts.

Industry observers note that the Series 12 offers up to 24 hours of everyday battery life, and Apple notes 15 minutes of charging can add up to 12 hours of battery. That makes it more manageable for overnight sleep tracking, but it still requires more planning than fitness trackers that last several days or longer on a single charge. “I’ve found the battery life is awesome for everyday use, but usually does need a charge every other day or so,” Aloin says.

Read More: Apple Watch Series 12 vs. Ultra 4.

The Google Fitbit Air gives you the quiet, distraction-free experience of a screenless wearable at a more approachable price point than premium recovery bands. The Fitbit Air tracks core metrics like activity, heart rate, sleep, and wellness trends over time, then sends that information to your phone.

Since there’s no screen, you’re not checking your wrist throughout the day. That makes it a strong option for anyone who wants to be more mindful about movement and sleep but doesn’t want a smartwatch. It’s also a good fit for people who are curious about screenless tracking but are not ready to commit to a more expensive platform. It offers a simpler, lower-pressure way to see whether passive health tracking actually helps your routine.

In a recent development, the Fitbit app is another advantage. Fitbit’s platform is approachable, especially for beginners, and tends to present health data in a way that feels less intimidating than more athlete-focused apps. That makes the Air a strong choice for casual customers who want guidance without performance overload.

According to recent reports, the main limitation is that a screenless budget tracker will not replace a running watch or smartwatch. You will not get the same real-time workout stats, app support, phone features, or advanced training analysis. But if you want affordable, low-distraction tracking, Fitbit Air is a compelling pick.

Sources indicate that the Coros Pace 4 is our best lightweight pick because it delivers serious training features in a watch that feels easy to wear. After testing the watch for two months, MH deputy features editor Carina Hsieh stated that it feels so lightweight that you forget it’s there. It’s especially appealing for runners and fitness-minded consumers who want more data than a basic tracker can provide but don’t want a bulky smartwatch.

Coros has built a strong reputation among runners because its watches tend to offer excellent battery life, practical training tools, and reliable GPS. The Pace 4 continues that tradition. “I was pleasantly surprised by how responsive and quick the GPS signal was on runs,” Hsieh said. She also noted that the watch had an exceptionally long battery life during her testing, and that she only had to charge it twice in two months.

For runners, the Pace 4 can track pace, distance, heart rate, route data, workouts, recovery, and training trends. Features like race predictions, virtual pacing, breadcrumb navigation, and personalized training tools make it feel like a strong contender for anyone who is a serious runner. It is also useful for people who cross-train, since it can handle gym workouts, cycling, walking, and other activities.

Sources indicate that A substantial reason to choose the Pace 4 over other smartwatches is that it feels purpose-built for fitness. You’re not paying for a huge app ecosystem or phone-like features. Instead, you’re getting a lightweight training watch that can help you understand your fitness, recovery, and progress.

Industry observers note that the Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 is the best fitness tracker for Android consumers, especially anyone with a Samsung Galaxy phone. It offers a polished smartwatch experience with robust health and fitness tools, making it a bit like an Android equivalent to the Apple Watch. WH beauty editor Nicole Saunders, who has tested multiple wearables over the years, says she usually struggles to wear trackers consistently because the bands were uncomfortable overnight. But the Galaxy Watch 9 changed that. “The band is surprisingly comfortable to wear and, dare I say, actually looks good,” she noted.

It has been revealed that this smartwatch tracks everyday activity, steps, heart rate, workouts, stress, sleep, and recovery-style metrics. It also includes Samsung’s Vitals feature, which monitors overnight patterns including heart rate, respiratory rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, and other sleep-related signals, then compares them against your personal baseline. Saunders says it took about a full week for her baseline to set up, and anything outside of her normal range appeared in orange in the app, making it easy to compare metrics and spot subtle changes over time.

It also tracks a wide range of exercise modes, and its running features are useful for people who want coaching-style tools. Samsung’s body composition measurement feature can also be helpful for observing trends over time, though the numbers should be treated as estimates rather than medical-grade measurements. Saunders also liked the sleep features, including sleep quality tracking and snore detection, which she found both funny and potentially useful for better understanding nighttime habits.

In a recent development, the watch pairs easily with Galaxy phones, and the Samsung Health app organizes fitness and wellness data in an approachable way. If you want a tracker that can monitor workouts in the morning, handle notifications during the day, and track sleep at night, the Galaxy Watch 9 is a strong choice. In her testing, Saunders found it to be stylish and effective, adding that it would make a great gift for someone starting a health journey or looking for more detailed insights.

Recent findings suggest that the Oura Ring 5 offers robust health and sleep tracking in the most discreet package of all the fitness trackers in this guide. If you don’t like wearing a watch around the clock or simply prefer jewelry over a wristband, Oura is the easiest fitness tracker to live with. In her review, WH associate editor Olivia Luppino said it’s the only fitness tracker she’s ever used that she hasn’t wanted to take off.

The Oura Ring’s biggest strength is passive health tracking. It’s designed to unobtrusively monitor your body in the background, and then translate that information into readiness, sleep, activity, stress, temperature, and recovery insights in an easy to use app. It can be especially helpful for people who want to understand how sleep, illness, stress, menstrual cycle changes, and daily habits affect energy.

Industry observers note that for sleep tracking, the Ring 5 is one of the more comfortable options since a ring is less bulky than a watch, and many people find it easier to wear overnight. The app also makes sleep data easy to understand, showing not just how long you slept but how restorative that sleep may have been.

The tradeoff is workout tracking. Oura can track activity and has improved its fitness features, but it’s still not the best choice for people who want real-time stats during runs, strength workouts, or cycling sessions. It can also interfere with grip during weightlifting and kettlebell training. If you want to glance at pace, heart rate, or intervals mid-workout, choose a watch. If you want discreet, all-day and all-night health tracking, choose a smart ring.

For runners, the Garmin Forerunner 570 sits in a sweet spot between advanced training watches and an everyday wearable. Garmin makes several excellent Forerunner models, but the 570 offers a mix of running metrics, GPS tools, recovery insights, smartwatch features, and comfortable wearability for runners who want more than the basics without jumping straight to flagship option.

The Forerunner 570 is designed to be useful for structured training with its capability to track runs, intervals, long runs, tempo sessions, races, recovery runs, and cross-training workouts. It also gives runners access to Garmin’s broader training ecosystem, including performance metrics, suggested workouts, recovery guidance, HRV status, sleep data, training readiness-style insights, and race-related tools. For someone training for a 5K, half marathon, marathon, or simply trying to become a more consistent runner, those features can be super useful.

Industry observers note that it has a bright AMOLED display, touchscreen support as well as physical buttons, a feature that’s especially notable for runners since touchscreens can sometimes be frustrating with sweat, rain, or gloves. Battery life varies from 8 hours to up to 10 days depending on how many features you’re using.

In a recent development, the biggest drawback is price. Though it’s not the priciest Forerunner offering out there, the Forerunner 570 is not inexpensive, and newer runners who only want pace, distance, and heart rate may be perfectly happy with a more affordable Forerunner model. But runners who want a capable watch they won’t outgrow, the 570 is a great option.

The Garmin Cirqa is the best screenless tracker for lovers of the Garmin fitness ecosystem, since it integrates seamlessly with Garmin’s other tech. It delivers health and activity tracking without adding another display to your life, and is especially well suited for anyone who wants to use Garmin Connect but doesn't want to wear a full Garmin watch all day long.

That makes Cirqa especially useful for athletes who already own a Garmin running, cycling, or outdoor watch. You may want to wear your Forerunner for workouts and during runs, but prefer something smaller and screen-free for sleep, recovery, or everyday tracking. The Cirqa fills that gap.

Sources indicate that it also has a cost advantage over some screenless competitors because it doesn’t require a subscription. That makes it appealing for Garmin loyalists who want ongoing tracking without committing to a monthly membership.

The Cirqa isn’t the best choice if you want live workout stats, on-wrist coaching, or a display for pace and distance, and a Garmin watch would be better for that. But as a low-distraction daily tracker that complements Garmin’s training platform, Cirqa is a welcome addition to the category.

The Google Fitbit Edge bridges the gap between a simple Fitbit band and a full smartwatch, making it a strong choice if you want a display but don’t want a bulkier smartwatch. It gives you a screen for checking stats, starting workouts, reviewing progress, and seeing basic information at a glance.

According to recent reports, compared with the Fitbit Air, the Edge is more interactive, compared with the Inspire, it’s a more advanced option, and compared with a Pixel Watch, it’s simpler to use and more fitness focused. It offers enough features to be useful throughout the day, tracking activity, workouts, sleep, heart-rate trends, and daily wellness data, while still keeping the overall experience lighter than a smartwatch. If you want a compact Google Fitbit tracker with a screen and stronger features than the entry-level models, the Edge is the best fit.

According to recent reports, A good heart rate monitor is one of the most crucial features to look for in a fitness tracker, whether you’re training seriously or just getting started. Heart rate data can help you better understand exercise intensity, track effort during workouts, and monitor resting heart rate over time, which can be a useful marker of cardiovascular fitness. While wrist-based trackers typically aren’t as precise as chest straps, they can still offer a helpful read on exertion levels during moderate to intense activity, according to a 2019 study in Cardiovascular Diagnosis & Therapy.

It has been revealed that sleep tracking can be a useful feature because sleep plays a major role in recovery, energy, mood, and overall performance. By tracking patterns like sleep duration, consistency, and overnight restlessness, a fitness tracker can help you spot habits that may be affecting how you feel the next day. Many models also break down sleep stages, show trends over time, and offer recovery or readiness insights based on your nightly data. While the numbers aren’t always perfect, they can provide a helpful starting point for understanding your routine and making small changes, like adjusting bedtime, limiting late caffeine, or improving sleep consistency.

Weight may not seem that crucial at first, but it matters when you’re wearing a fitness tracker all day and night. A larger, heavier model can feel more noticeable over time, especially during sleep or long workouts. There’s no single ideal size, and the best option will depend on how you plan to use it.

If you run, hike, or spend a lot of time outdoors, it may be worth choosing a more durable model, even if it’s slightly bulkier. For everyday wear, walking, strength training, or mostly indoor workouts, a lighter, lower-profile tracker may be more comfortable. Ultimately, the right fit comes down to your activity level, wrist size, and what you’ll actually want to keep wearing.

Many of the best fitness trackers can run for days or even weeks on a single charge, such as the Whoop 5.0. But battery doesn't always equate to quality, given that an option like the Apple Watch Series 12 needs to be charged every day and it’s still one of our absolute favorites. Ultimately it comes down to how a trackers charging needs will fit into your routine.

Sources indicate that as with all tech, you want a fitness tracker that’s easy to use. If your new tracker isn’t intuitive for you to set up or use daily, you’re far less likely to use it consistently. Ultimately, the only way to know for sure is to try it out yourself to see if it works for you. That's why it’s smart to buy a fitness tracker with a generous return policy.

It has been revealed that I’ve been a certified personal trainer for more than a decade, and together with other Women’s Health editors, I’m constantly testing the latest fitness trackers across key factors like durability, comfort, features, and accuracy. We tested them during our workouts, on our runs, in Pilates class, and more. And of course, we tested them during sleep. Whether you’re training regularly or just want something for everyday activity tracking, the models we tested for the latest upgrade range from basic fitness trackers to powerful smartwatches and everything in between.

In the Berkshires, an Intensely Yellow Kitchen Is Anything but Mellow in This Lakeside Cottage

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1399 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that “I personally would not want this yellow in my kitchen,” notes Jess Cooney.
  • According to recent reports, cooney’s clients didn’t blink at the bold idea.
  • Industry observers note that cooney’s clients weren’t initially convinced by reclaimed brick flooring in the entryway, but Cooney’s team proved convincing—they believed the space needed a worn palette to counterbalance the intensely yellow kitchen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that “I personally would not want this yellow in my kitchen,” notes Jess Cooney. It’s a cheeky comment about the beaming hue she herself chose for clients in the Berkshires—a color that defines their entire lakeside home, one she calls the diva of the whole project, requiring (no, demanding) decisions in every square foot to balance out its intensity.

According to recent reports, cooney’s clients didn’t blink at the bold idea. Unusually carefree for a couple with high-powered jobs, they gave the AD PRO Directory designer free license to create. The bungalow was purchased as a weekend retreat from life in Fresh York, but even before paint swatches were discussed, the kitchen was a sticking point. “The kitchen was crazy—it was this tiny little makeshift kitchen,” notes Cooney.

Industry observers note that cooney’s clients weren’t initially convinced by reclaimed brick flooring in the entryway, but Cooney’s team proved convincing—they believed the space needed a worn palette to counterbalance the intensely yellow kitchen. Much to their clients’ delight, it worked beautifully. A Croft House Morro Credenza with leather-front doors anchors the space, topped with a vintage lamp from Millerton Antiques Center and set beneath an unknown artwork from Brimfield Flea Market.

Sources indicate that cooney opted to stain wood-paneled walls in custom blue and brown stains from Rubio Monocoat, allowing rustic grains to shine through. Atop a Jaipur Hazan rug, an upholstered George Smith Emma Ottoman anchors the room and is accompanied by a set of armchairs and a velvet mordoré sofa from Lawson-Fenning. A 20th-century oil painting by Paul Berg hangs above the reworked fireplace, while in the corner, above a Charles Dudouyt side table, hangs a vintage painting sourced from The Little Store in Massachusetts.

In a recent development, “We just decided to kind of lean into it and go almost in a maximalist way,” indicates Cooney of the dining room’s focal point, a painting by K.G. Narendra Babu that inspired the home’s many colors. For the inside of a Four Hands Camila Sideboard, they commissioned artisan Joel Haynes to hand-paint a leafy pattern. A Hubbardton Forge Disq fixture hangs above a custom Bossi dining table surrounded with Tribute Modern Dining Chairs from Craft Associates.

In a recent development, the husband, an English lawyer, craved a small cabin in the woods, while the wife, an Italian who loves cooking, wanted a home large enough to host intimate gatherings. “This house was a happy compromise,” notes the husband. But while the home spans three levels and around 4,500 square feet, the main floor measured just about 1,000. The kitchen, in a cramped corner, didn’t cut it.

According to recent reports, cooney’s team reconfigured a few walls. They collapsed oversized closets in the entryway, shrinking the space to a slimmer mudroom while letting the entire layout exhale, expanding the footprint of the semi-open cooking area. The room is now the proper heart of the home, and its bright yellow cabinets aren’t shy about it.

Cabinets with glass windows were fabricated by Westek Architectural Woodworking and feature an array of white porcelain that punctuates and calms the intensely painted millwork; the pieces were all sourced from shops in the Berkshires, including Millerton Antiques, All that Jazz, and Montage Antiques.

“It’s the diva of the project,” notes Cooney of the yellow Benjamin Moore paint used throughout the kitchen, a choice that influenced nearly all palettes throughout the home. Ceilings, walls, and upper cabinets were painted in Farrow & Ball’s New White.

The kitchen island is topped with a wooden counter and is paired with Amber Interiors Cade Counter Stools in walnut. A set of Matthew Fairbank Allegro Pendants hang above the island.

The saturated hue, Benjamin Moore’s Glen Ridge Gold, wasn’t a choice made on a whim. Like many colors peppering the home, it was inspired by a painting by Chennai-based artist K.G. Narendra Babu that now hangs in the couple’s dining room. The artwork was given to the couple by a family member who worked in India, and it features an array of folk and musical motifs.

“The whole point of the project is that it’s bright and energetic and deeply relaxing at the same time,” notes Cooney. “That was the trust that they put in us—to believe that both could happen.”.

In a recent development, the architecture itself lacked a definitive style. Light traces of Arts & Crafts style gave Cooney a point of view to reinvent existing character. A fireplace in the living room is now reimagined with glazed brick Clé tiles, their dappled surface cladding the surround with clean lines and a crafted look; a custom stain allowed wood-paneled walls to bear rustic grains but in modern blue-green tones.

It has been revealed that to expand the kitchen’s footprint, Cooney reclaimed space from unnecessarily large closets in the entryway. Her team moved the wall to install smaller, but equally useful, cabinets that turn the space into a mudroom. The custom millwork, crafted by Westek Architectural Woodworking and painted in Farrow & Ball’s Blue Gray, complements a vintage rug and a built-in bench.

It has been revealed that A custom walnut vanity injects warmth as an alternative to a colder stone. Cooney’s team used a boat sealer to coat and protect the walnut, giving the material a high-gloss finish. A fabric shade made with Eric Kuster’s Micha 002 textile occupies the space that might traditionally feature a mirror. “You can kind of break a rule and have it be playful and fun, especially in a powder bath,” states Cooney, noting that a mirror hangs on the side wall instead. The wallcovering is Pierre Frey’s Uberon print.

Recent findings suggest that cooney describes an almost cottagey feel in the primary, thanks to a walnut Flora Bed by Jacob May, which was locally made and turned by hand, layered with cozy and textural textiles like Parachute Home’s Hand Stitched Cotton Quilt. Gentle patterns add to the mix through a Scandinavian kilim with geometric design from Rug & Kilim, and light drapes made with a Best Buds textile by Kerry Joyce.

Making the most of existing features, light touches to the bathroom reimagined the space, like painting existing wainscoting in Farrow & Ball’s Tanner’s Brown, and covering the walls in a botanical House of Hackney Herbarium wallpaper. For a touch of texture, Cooney also layered vintage rugs and set an antique Victorian bamboo chair in the corner below the window.

With a view over the living room, Cooney states the lofted floor is like a little escape within the small cottage. Leaning into the cozy feel, the team went with a layered look. A brass chest anchors the space, paired with a black armchair owned by the clients, which was reupholstered with a burgundy fabric from Abraham Moon & Sons, and a Lawson-Fenning Morro Sectional in a linen blend.

According to recent reports, the clients’ only real hesitation was a bit of a surprise: the reclaimed brick Cooney specified for the mudroom. It is laid in a herringbone pattern with colors that appeared to shift across the surface. That yellow kitchen? Totally fine. But the expressive bricks? Too dramatic. “We relied on the team’s judgement, and this feature is now one of our most favorite parts of the home,” says the husband, noting how guests often compliment the mudroom.

Recent findings suggest that “I feel like this house is kind of us unchecked,” claims Cooney of her clients’ trust. “No one checked us, so we were allowed to do the fullest extent of what we wanted to do.” Her clients could easily have staged their own diva moment after the cabinets were painted in screaming yellow, before everything else around it fell into place around it; but they let the vision come into full focus.

As if cantilevered over the hill, a screened-in porch is the best of both worlds. “You don’t have to have everything be indoor-outdoor in a covered porch—you can really pull the inside out there and not worry so much,” indicates Cooney, nodding to choices like Henning Kjaernulf dining chairs from the 1960s purchased from Lone Fox. And while most might use a lighter color in this space, Cooney chose a deeper Farrow & Ball Hopper Head paint for the walls and window frames, which she says helps punctuate the view in a beautiful way.

The view overlooking the Berkshires.

Hyundai is shaking up its 2027 electric vehicle lineup: Here’s what’s changing

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hyundai’s US electric vehicle lineup will look a bit different in 2027, including the fresh IONIQ 6 N, a new range-topping IONIQ 9 trim, and a handful of minor updates to the IONIQ 5.
  • Hyundai announced its 2027 model-year changes on Wednesday, including the upcoming IONIQ 6 N and a few slight changes to the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9.
  • While Hyundai discontinued the standard IONIQ 6, it added the high-performance IONIQ 6 N for the 2027 lineup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hyundai’s US electric vehicle lineup will look a bit different in 2027, including the fresh IONIQ 6 N, a new range-topping IONIQ 9 trim, and a handful of minor updates to the IONIQ 5.

Hyundai announced its 2027 model-year changes on Wednesday, including the upcoming IONIQ 6 N and a few slight changes to the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9.

While Hyundai discontinued the standard IONIQ 6, it added the high-performance IONIQ 6 N for the 2027 lineup.

The IONIQ 6 N is Hyundai’s second performance EV, following the IONIQ 5 N. Powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, the electric sports car delivers a combined 641 hp and 568 lb-ft of torque.

Hyundai said the IONIQ 6 N can sprint from 0 to 60 mph in 3.2 seconds, beating the IONIQ 5 N at 3.25 seconds.

Like the IONIQ 5 N, it also includes fun added features, like N e-Shift and an N Active Sound+ system that simulates the sounds and sensations of a traditional gas-powered sports car with an 8-speed dual-clutch transmission.

Industry observers note that it uses an 84 kWh battery that provides up to 245 miles of pure electric driving range. Thanks to its 800V ultra-fast charging architecture, the IONIQ 6 N can charge from 10% to 80% in about 18 minutes using a 350 kW DC fast charger.

Like Hyundai’s other electric vehicles, it comes standard with a native NACS charging port and a CCS adapter.

The 2027 IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 are mostly carryover models with a few minor changes, while the IONIQ 5 N remains the same as the 2026 model year.

Changes to the IONIQ 5 for the 2027 model year include roof rails, which are now available on the SEL trim and above; previously, they were only available on the XRT and Limited trims.

Hyundai HomeLink will be available exclusively on the Limited trim, rather than SEL and above, in the current 2026 model year, while the Cargo Cover will be offered as an Accessory only.

Regarding color options, the Gravity Gold Matte and Sage Silver Matte will no longer be available for the 2027 IONIQ 5.

The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 starts at $35,250, making it one of the most affordable EVs in the US.

According to recent reports, that’s for the standard-range IONIQ 5 SE with an EPA-estimated range of up to 245 miles. The extended-range SE RWD model is $2,500 more, starting at $37,750, and offers up to 318 miles of range.

Hyundai’s three-row SUV also received a handful of updates. The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 9 will be available with a newly introduced Calligraphy Black Ink trim, while the Calligraphy Design will no longer be offered.

The 2027 IONIQ 9 Calligraphy and Calligraphy Black Ink trims gain a Virtual Gear Shift and heated third-row seats. All variants also gain a Tailgate Emergency Lamp.

It has been revealed that on the one hand... the Ioniq5 is due for an update. On the other... I still absolutely love the way it looks, and notice just about every one I pass on the road.

Hyundai has yet to announce prices for the 2027 model. The base 2026 IONIQ 9 S starts at $58,995 and offers an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 335 miles.

The previous top-spec Performance Calligraphy Design AWD started at $76,490, so you can expect the latest Calligraphy Black Ink to be around the same, if not even more.

Mauviel's Copper Cookware Is 25% Off For Black Friday

💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are a few covetable luxury goods you’ll see pop up again and again in AD’s home tours: a Moccamaster coffee maker, a Nordic Knots rug, and Mauviel copper cookware, to name a few.
  • Industry observers note that I’m a recent convert; I bought my Mauviel frying pan mostly to elevate the aesthetic of my kitchen, with a suspicion that the tool would also function as a fantastic piece of cookware, particularly for my beloved morning ritual of frying up an egg for breakfast.
  • Recent findings suggest that that excellent cooking capability is largely due to the construction and craftsmanship of the goods, which have a long history as a French culinary staple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are a few covetable luxury goods you’ll see pop up again and again in AD’s home tours: a Moccamaster coffee maker, a Nordic Knots rug, and Mauviel copper cookware, to name a few. As seen in this Sag Harbor home, this Parisian pied-à-terre, this Westchester residence, and this Connecticut country retreat, Mauviel is something of a status symbol in kitchens. Much like a Le Creuset Dutch oven out on display, spying a few copper pans from the French brand hanging from a rail signals that “Great Taste Lives Here.” And this week marks a good opportunity to join the club, with Mauviel sets and individual pieces up to 30% off for Black Friday at Williams Sonoma and on Shop.

Industry observers note that I’m a recent convert; I bought my Mauviel frying pan mostly to elevate the aesthetic of my kitchen, with a suspicion that the tool would also function as a fantastic piece of cookware, particularly for my beloved morning ritual of frying up an egg for breakfast. Of course it does. Unlike some of my ceramic pans that catch and dry out an egg, the Mauviel has given me no trouble, delivering me the most perfect eggs to date I’ve ever cooked. Even against my stainless-steel pans (which I do love very much), these heat a bit more promptly and evenly.

Recent findings suggest that that excellent cooking capability is largely due to the construction and craftsmanship of the goods, which have a long history as a French culinary staple. Mauviel has made copper cookware since 1830 in Villedieu-les-Poêles, a town in Normandy with an enduring history of copper manufacturing; the pieces are still handcrafted there. As far as their makeup, the M’150 B pieces are, for example, 1.5 millimeters thick and constructed of a 90% polished copper exterior and a 10% stainless-steel interior. They heat evenly; are immediately responsive to heat adjustments; and work on gas, electric, and ceramic cooktops.

The pans partners with a copper kettle on the stove in this Portland manse by Jessica Helgerson.

According to recent reports, the copper treasures do, however, require care. They’re not nonstick pots and pans, so you need a little oil or butter to get any slip. They’re hand-wash only, and Mauviel advises against using them for long stretches on high heat or leaving them empty on a hot burner. I don’t polish mine, simply because I don’t own any copper polish. The wear indicates quickly, and I like that, though if AD were shooting my house, maybe I’d like it less.

Recent findings suggest that the Black Friday markdowns run across the line: my copper fry pan is going for $280 in the 10-inch size (25% off), a 2.5-quart sauce pan is $450 (29% off), and a 15-piece cookware set is $3,000 (32% off). For anyone who cooks every day, it’s a hard gift to beat. I, for one, now can’t imagine frying my eggs any other way.

#190233. Tesla confirms rare fresh delivery of 50 Semi electric trucks in Chicago

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1020 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tesla confirms rare fresh delivery of 50 Semi electric trucks in Chicago

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1020 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla has confirmed a new batch of Tesla Semi deliveries, with its official Semi account saying today that “Chicago’s first 50 Semis” are on their way to the city.
  • Tesla doesn’t disclose Semi deliveries, and it claims its latest Nevada factory can build 50,000 of them a year.
  • The post, published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, demonstrates four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla has confirmed a new batch of Tesla Semi deliveries, with its official Semi account saying today that “Chicago’s first 50 Semis” are on their way to the city.

It’s a rare data point. Tesla doesn’t disclose Semi deliveries, and it claims its latest Nevada factory can build 50,000 of them a year.

The post, published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, demonstrates four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.

Hello Windy CityChicago’s first 50 Semis en route for delivery pic.twitter.com/75kig8yWsb.

But the only 50-truck Semi order tied to Chicago belongs to HMD Trucking. The family-owned carrier was founded in Chicago in 1998, runs more than 650 trucks (almost all diesel), and ordered 50 Semis right after Tesla’s production event in September.

HMD took its first truck on November 2 and says it’s the first Tesla Semi registered in Illinois. COO Michael Mahler said Tesla “has been transparent with us regarding the capabilities of Semi every step of the way.”.

Sources indicate that the manufacturer ran a Semi for more than 4,000 miles over the summer and averaged 1.74 kWh per mile, right in line with Tesla’s 1.7 kWh/mile claim. The first trucks will mostly handle local runs around Chicago, and HMD is installing its own chargers there since Tesla’s Megacharger network is still concentrated along the I-5 and I-10 corridors in the West.

Owner Henry Malukas told MotorTrend the deal is worth about $15 million. That’s roughly $300,000 per truck, in line with the ~$290,000 Long Range pricing we reported when the first truck came off the high-volume line and a long way from the $180,000 Tesla advertised in 2017.

Here’s the problem: it’s nearly impossible to tell how many Semis Tesla is actually building.

Tesla released volume production at its Sparks, Nevada factory on September 24, after pushing the ramp out of 2025. It says the 1.8 million sq ft plant is built for 50,000 trucks a year. But it never gave a ramp schedule, and its quarterly production and delivery reports only count “passenger vehicles sold to customers.” The Semi isn’t in there.

So we’re left with proxies. Tesla states its Semi fleet has over 98% uptime, without saying how big that fleet is. Before this year, the largest Semi fleet was PepsiCo’s, at 86 trucks in 2024. California’s truck voucher program received 965 Semi applications between January 2025 and February 2026, which points to real demand but says nothing about output.

The order book is the other clue. Einride ordered 500 Semis in August, WattEV has 370 on order, IMC Logistics wants 50 for California, and the ZET SCALE alliance picked Tesla as main supplier for 2,500 trucks. And now HMD’s 50 are rolling into Chicago, one of the first Semi fleets that will have to deal with a Midwest winter. Wisconsin’s Paper Transport has also been piloting a Semi in the Chicago market since the summer.

None of that adds up to a production rate, but it does look like Tesla is slowly ramping up deliveries.

Tesla keeps the Semi numbers vague on purpose. It’s happy to talk about a 50,000-truck-a-year factory, and it posts hero shots when a batch ships, but it won’t give the one number that indicates whether the factory is anywhere close to that.

I think the semi is going to be a major seller but its going to take some time to produce enough of them and for companies to gather enough data. Once the investment is justified, there will be customers and repeat customers. After that, it will only be a matter of time before other electric semi truck manufacturers start popping up with offerings and thats a good thing for everyone.

The 50,000 figure is what makes the Semi look like a real business to investors instead of a niche program that took nine years to get going. Tesla has a long history of quoting capacity long before it reaches it, so we shouldn’t treat “built for 50,000” as anything more than a ceiling.

Our read: Tesla is still far from that 50,000 rate. Fifty trucks for one customer is 0.1% of a year at full capacity, and if Tesla were shipping in large volumes, a single 50-unit batch wouldn’t get its own post. But the ramp has clearly started, the order book is real, and it’s plausible Tesla gets into the thousands by the end of the year.

It has been revealed that good for HMD, too. A 650-truck diesel fleet in a cold market is exactly the kind of customer the Semi has to win. Malukas admitted “we don’t have real numbers yet” on savings, and HMD’s own blog is fairly sober about cost and winter range. Local routes, depot charging and a Chicago winter is the right way to find out. It all sounds plausible for the Tesla Semi.

Tech Report: ‘I Started Strength Training at 74. At 78, I Can Deadlift 132 Lbs—Here’s How.’

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1162 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if there’s one thing I’ve learned as I’ve gotten older, it’s that being active and being strong aren’t necessarily the same thing.
  • Industry observers note that I wanted everyday activities, like climbing stairs, carrying groceries, and getting up off the floor, to feel easier.
  • In a recent development, after a few weeks, I gradually incorporated 5- to 8-lb dumbbells into the movements, and a month or two later, I noticed a real difference in my strength: I could do more repetitions, lift even heavier weights, and move with greater confidence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if there’s one thing I’ve learned as I’ve gotten older, it’s that being active and being strong aren’t necessarily the same thing. For most of my life, I’d been recreationally active, and had loved kayaking, swimming, and taking my dog on long walks. I’d never done any kind of structured strength training, until right before my 75th birthday. One day, I was sitting on a curb outside my house, and when it was time to stand up, I couldn’t. I felt embarrassed, and the idea of falling and not being able to get up or being in a situation where I couldn’t take care of myself was scary.

Industry observers note that I wanted everyday activities, like climbing stairs, carrying groceries, and getting up off the floor, to feel easier. I also wanted to trust my body more, and feel confident in my ability to handle whatever life threw my way. So, I joined Aspire Athletic Club, a gym near my home in Schenectady, Newly introduced York, and began working out once a week with the owner, Chris Wertman. In the beginning, even simple movements were challenging, so I started with basic bodyweight exercises like the box squat, step-up, and bird dog. The focus was on learning proper form and getting comfortable with the movements.

In a recent development, after a few weeks, I gradually incorporated 5- to 8-lb dumbbells into the movements, and a month or two later, I noticed a real difference in my strength: I could do more repetitions, lift even heavier weights, and move with greater confidence. It was so encouraging to see the hard work pay off, and it motivated me to keep going. About a year into consistent training, I was feeling stronger and ready to take on more. I began training full-body twice a week and incorporated more challenging exercises like squat variations, the walking lunge, weighted glute bridge, and chest fly to build overall strength.

I’d never deadlifted before, so seeing someone my age lift with that kind of strength was incredibly inspiring. That decision marked the beginning of a latest chapter in my strength training journey—I told my new trainer of about six months, Jack Tyree, that I wanted to lift heavier weights and try deadlifting. I even began training for my gym’s upcoming annual deadlift exhibition, which was in eight months.

Since I’d just been training with dumbbells, I tried working with a kettlebell while I got comfortable with the movement and proper technique. As I got stronger and more confident, I graduated to the barbell and continued adding more weight each week. Then, this past May, I deadlifted 132 lbs for a single rep at the exhibition, setting a personal record. I never imagined I’d be able to do something like that, but I was so proud of how strong I’d become—and I was excited to see how much further I could push myself.

Sources indicate that six months after the exhibition, I now strength train three days a week: one day focused on upper body, one on lower body, and one dedicated to mobility and balance. Jack still programs all my workouts, and every session includes six to eight exercises, with 3 or 4 sets of 6 to 8 reps each. I use a mix of free weights and weight machines, and some of my go-to moves include the farmer’s carry, curtsy lunge, lat pulldown, scapular pushup, squat, and bench press. Deadlifts are still my favorite; I can now do three reps at 132 lbs, which I’m really proud of.

According to recent reports, outside the gym, I love getting outside and staying active, so I walk a few miles with my dog every day for my cardiovascular health. In addition to mobility and balance work at the gym, I also try to stretch at home whenever I can to ease muscle soreness and improve my range of motion, especially in my shoulders and hips.

I know nutrition is an key part of recovery too. Although I don’t follow a strict nutrition proposal or count macros, I try to eat protein at every meal to support muscle growth. Usually, it’s chicken, red meat, or a scoop of protein powder mixed into my morning oatmeal. I also prioritize whole foods and aim to incorporate a variety of fruits and vegetables throughout the day.

It has been revealed that when I first started strength training, I didn’t know where to begin. So, having someone guide me through the movements, teach me proper form, and help me build strength safely made all the difference. My trainers have helped me recognize what I’m capable of, push beyond what I thought was possible, and progress at a pace that feels right. They also create workouts that challenge me while keeping my goals in mind. Having their support and encouragement has given me the confidence to try things I never imagined I could do. Whether it’s deadlifting heavy weights, bench pressing a barbell, or taking less rest between working sets, my trainers have taught me not to put a ceiling on what I think I can accomplish.

Recent findings suggest that before I strength trained, I felt weak and unsteady, but I didn’t give up and accept that I’d feel like that for the rest of my life. In some ways, I completely started over with exercise at 74 because I tried something brand new—and that’s affected my life outside of the gym.

According to recent reports, now, at 78, I feel stronger than ever; I can get up off the floor with ease, carry my own groceries into the house, shovel snow, garden, and play sports with my grandchildren. These are things I want to keep doing independently, and having the strength to do them confidently means the world to me. While I love lifting weights and hitting new PRs, the greatest reward is how much easier everyday life has become.

Learning to lift in my mid-70s wasn’t easy, and building that strength didn’t happen overnight, but I kept showing up, putting in the work, and gradually accomplishing what I once never thought was possible. Now, as I approach 80, I’m still getting stronger, and I want other women to know they’re never too old to get started, and they may be capable of far more than they realize. If I can go from struggling to get up from a curb to deadlifting 132 pounds, who knows what else is possible?

Morning Minute: Jensen Returns, Markets Soar (Except Crypto)

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (520 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Decrypt

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner.
  • Six days after Nvidia’s board chair told investors “the Nvidia board does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” the board voted unanimously to reinstate him as president, CEO and director, effective immediately.
  • According to recent reports, nvidia shares rose 33% to around $167, adding roughly a trillion dollars of market value in a session.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

Six days after Nvidia’s board chair told investors “the Nvidia board does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” the board voted unanimously to reinstate him as president, CEO and director, effective immediately.

According to recent reports, nvidia shares rose 33% to around $167, adding roughly a trillion dollars of market value in a session. Huang’s personal net worth climbed about $36.6 billion on his 3.5% stake, moving him to 13th on the Forbes global list. Short sellers took roughly $12.2 billion in paper losses, their worst single day since at least 2019, which wiped out the $10.5 billion they had booked the prior week.

The stock market absolutely ripped on the news. The Nasdaq closed up 6.51% at 24,089, its best day since April 2025. The S&P gained 4.7%, the Dow was +3%, and the VIX collapsed 25.8% to 26.62.

Sources indicate that bitcoin went along with the ride—for a few hours. It touched $63,929 intraday, up 5.1%, then spent the afternoon handing it back and finished near $61,000, barely up on the day. The ETFs used the pump to exit more, with BTC ETFs seeing another $570M in outflows on the day.

ETH and other majors also closed red. Alts gave back their gains. And the CMC top 20 index managed just 0.20% gain.

That’s a 19 to 1 ratio between what the Nasdaq captured and what Bitcoin kept, on the same catalyst, on the same day. Pain for the crypto bulls.

What makes it even more painful, is that crypto fell with AI stocks the whole way down, and the standard explanation was that both trade on the same liquidity and the same risk appetite. Monday tested that and the correlation fell through. The AI trade got a catalyst and markets bounced. Crypto didn’t bounce with it.

As for Nvidia’s reversal decision itself, questions remain to say the least. The board claims it was satisfied with Huang’s “candor and ability to lead,” and that input from senior U.S. officials left it confident his return “poses no national security risk.” Trump publicly pushed for it and mentioned the board had sought assurance on the espionage allegations. What actually changed between November 17 and November 23 hasn’t been explained. The independent directors’ investigation is still open, and Nvidia is now standing up a board committee for national security and export-control oversight plus recruiting a chief compliance officer.

Perhaps answers will trickle out over time. The AI trade may not need them anyway. And crypto, well, it's in its own world right now, waiting for its own catalysts (likely quantum-related). But it’s very unclear that catalyst is coming in 2026, and it’s becoming clear that many are not interested in waiting for the answers….

Tesla extends Cybertruck production to late summer 2027 amid fan backlash

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1115 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elon Musk now indicates Tesla will keep building the Cybertruck “through the end of summer 2027” to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” That buys the electric pickup roughly two to three more months, five days after Tesla first revealed it was killing it.
  • The reprieve lands as a growing number of Tesla’s own fans push back on the decision, and on what it notes about Tesla’s future as a firm that sells cars to people.
  • In a recent development, on November 6, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas “around the middle of next year” to make room for Cybercab.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk now indicates Tesla will keep building the Cybertruck “through the end of summer 2027” to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” That buys the electric pickup roughly two to three more months, five days after Tesla first revealed it was killing it.

The reprieve lands as a growing number of Tesla’s own fans push back on the decision, and on what it notes about Tesla’s future as a firm that sells cars to people.

In a recent development, on November 6, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas “around the middle of next year” to make room for Cybercab. On November 9, he wrote the line would shut “in about 8 months” and that Tesla would “have to return deposits for a lot of people.” Now it’s the end of summer.

In order to work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog, production will be extended through the end of summer 2027.

The reasons have moved around just as much. First it was factory space, then “a very limited number of smart, dedicated people,” then the “opportunity cost” of the truck’s complexity. We went through each of them: Tesla is ending the Cybertruck as sales stall at about 10% of blueprint, Musk’s demand claim doesn’t survive the numbers, and Musk admitted Tesla doesn’t have the talent to run more than one vehicle program.

Recent findings suggest that and the “backlog” is one Tesla built itself. Before the announcement, the truck was selling at a pace of roughly 30,000 units a year, about 10% of the 250,000 Tesla planned for, on a line with over 125,000 units of installed capacity. Telling people the truck is going away creates a last-call rush. That’s not demand Tesla was missing before.

Tesla also raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10% the same day and paused orders for the base Dual Motor. The cheapest Cybertruck you can order is now $92,490, up from $69,990 in early August.

Industry observers note that some of the people in that backlog have been waiting a while. Several cheering in Musk’s replies say they’re still waiting on the $59,990 Cybertruck Tesla sold for “10 days only” in February. One asked whether Tesla will prioritize Premium and Cyberbeast orders over theirs. Musk didn’t answer.

It has been revealed that the most telling replies weren’t about the truck. Chuck Cook, one of the best-known FSD testers in the Tesla community, quote-tweeted Musk asking him to “change your mind,” adding: “Cybercab won’t haul my bees.”.

Another longtime Tesla supporter, Phil Trubey, asked for “a vehicle roadmap post end of summer 2027,” followed by: “Will Tesla make any other vehicle?”.

That’s the right question, and Tesla hasn’t revealed a single upcoming consumer vehicle to answer it. Tesla started 2026 with five consumer vehicle programs: Model S, Model X, Model 3, Model Y, and Cybertruck. It ended Model S and Model X production in the spring, citing “autonomy.” The Cybertruck goes next. By fall 2027, Tesla’s consumer lineup will be the Model 3 and Model Y, two vehicles that released in 2017 and 2020.

Tesla’s answer to the affordable car it promised for years was stripped-down “Standard” versions of those same two vehicles. In China, its second-biggest market, Tesla turned Giga Shanghai into an export hub, and domestic retail sales crashed 66% in October to the lowest level in over four years.

Recent findings suggest that even Unplugged Performance, the biggest Tesla tuner around, offered to take the Cybertruck line off Tesla’s hands and pay a license fee. People want this truck built. Tesla doesn’t.

We’ve been warning about this for years, and for years we got called haters for it.

According to recent reports, the pattern has been clear since Tesla swapped its affordable car aims for Robotaxi in 2024. No latest consumer platform. Model S and X killed “for autonomy.” Cybertruck killed “for Cybercab.” A Roadster pitched as a thruster stunt nine years after its unveiling. Every product decision points away from selling cars to people and toward robotaxis and Optimus, two businesses that don’t generate meaningful revenue today.

I am beginning to suspect that Elon does not always tell the truth.

As long as we have an economic climate that allows massive amounts of money to be made off of speculation as opposed to actual product, future bots and robotaxis have a great deal of value whether they actually become viable or not.

A two-to-three-month extension doesn’t change any of that. It’s a gesture to the loudest part of the fan base, and it happens to let Tesla sell a few thousand more trucks at prices up to 10% higher than last week. Fine. But the people who bought into Tesla’s mission to accelerate the world’s transition to sustainable energy are now realizing that mission was quietly rewritten, and the word “sustainable” didn’t make the cut.

Recent findings suggest that tesla is becoming a firm that sells two aging EVs to fund a bet on autonomy. That might work out for shareholders. We have our doubts, given Tesla is still behind Waymo by every public metric. But it’s a lot less exciting for the people who wanted the next great Tesla car.

The question for fans now: when the Model 3 and Model Y get their own “opportunity cost” post on X, will anyone actually be surprised?

15 Best Places to Buy Bedding, Editor Picks (2026)

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sheets get slept in every night and washed every week (in theory) which means it doesn’t take long to learn which ones hold up under use.
  • Each brand earned its spot for a reason, whether that’s price, a cooling fabric, an unusually wide color range, or embroidery done by hand.
  • For bedding basics that won’t damage the budget, Quince is our first stop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sheets get slept in every night and washed every week (in theory) which means it doesn’t take long to learn which ones hold up under use. Every retailer here comes recommended by an AD editor or contributor who has lived with the bedding at home for a long stretch: flannel kept on the bed through May, linen hauled to a communal laundromat and back, or a sheet set that survives a dog digging in every night.

Each brand earned its spot for a reason, whether that’s price, a cooling fabric, an unusually wide color range, or embroidery done by hand. Rest assured: they’re all comfy.

For bedding basics that won’t damage the budget, Quince is our first stop. Its European Linen Sheet Set earned our pick for the best affordable linen sheets, and senior shopping editor Nashia Baker has recently added the brand to her list of favorites. “The price point is unbeatable, and I love that they offer bedding sets in beautiful colorways and a variety of fabric options,” she indicates. “The quality is also impressive, especially considering the affordability.”.

According to recent reports, made from 100% European flax, the sheets cost a fraction of what competitors charge, thanks in part to Quince’s direct-to-consumer model which skips traditional retail markups. “I love its airy nature along with the gorgeous Bordeaux color that complements the rest of my decor,” says Baker. The bedding range extends to quilts and coverlets, , and the brand’s down comforter also made our ranking of the best comforters.

It has been revealed that anyone who has paused a Nancy Meyers movie to study the bedroom should start with Serena & Lily. The brand is based in Sausalito, California, but its textured, breezy bedding and decor would look right at home on any coast, Nantucket included. The range covers lightweight linen and crisp cotton percale in pale colors and easygoing prints.

According to recent reports, of all the bedding Baker has tested, the Nantucket Stripe Sheet Set ranks near the top for its light weight and “worn-in texture,” which keeps the linen soft instead of scratchy. The ruffle trim keeps her bed from looking too plain. “The striped mink print does give a seaside vibe, but it’s been neutral enough to layer with any color bed cover without clashing with the rest of my minimal, romantic decor over the few months I’ve tested the set,” she adds. For a top layer, there’s the scalloped Baywood Quilt, which Alpert likes as a light blanket for “when you want to throw something over while you read your favorite Emily Henry book in bed.”.

In a recent development, boll & Branch sheets arrive feeling as if they’ve already been through several wash cycles, without the fraying or pilling that usually comes with that. Contributor Rachel Fletcher tested the brand’s percale, Supima cotton, flannel, and linen, but its signature sateen stood out most for its long-staple cotton and a soft, smooth finish. “That extra-soft feel, paired with the lovely, cooling properties, make them feel like the luxury sheets they are,” she claims. Converts can outfit the rest of the room too, with Boll & Branch’s mattresses and bedroom furniture.

It has been revealed that brooklinen started out selling two things, cotton percale and sateen sheets, and has since added cashmere, brushed flannel, and a long list of prints. Pieces come in bundled sets or one at a time, and prices land between the budget brands and the luxury labels. Our editors keep coming back to the linen sheets, which they use in every season.

Recent findings suggest that “Since I don’t live my life on a Greek island, I thought white linen sheets year-round might be a slightly bold move, but the nature of the fiber is versatile and temperature regulating,” indicates AD contributor Madeleine Luckel, who tested the Core Sheet Set. Fletcher sleeps on the Luxe Sheet Set and credits it with keeping her cool. “I’m a hot sleeper with sensitive skin, and they’re really cool on my skin at night, which is a huge relief,” she says. “I love the breathability of these sheets.”.

Few bedding brands have tied their name to sustainability as closely as Coyuchi. Its linen sheets are made from certified organic French flax grown without synthetic fertilizers or pesticides, and the brand also offers percale, sateen, and flannel sheets. The earthy color palette is a selling point on its own.

“I love the color, which is what drew me to these sheets in the first place,” claims Sam Cochran, global features editor. “They’re the perfect brown—a tad auburn, ever so slightly timeworn in palette.”.

Shopping writer Julia Harrison and contributor Kate McGregor agree: Garnet Hill is their “secret spot” for bedding. Harrison is devoted to the flannel sheets and admits she leaves them on the bed through May because “they’re so soft, I’d rather suffer in my own sweat than switch them out.” The ticking stripe is “perfectly classic—like a true vintage piece, but not actually vintage…that might be tough sell in the bedding department.” Alpert also loves her flannel pick, a duvet cover that “signals a cottagecore moment without going over the top.” Paired with her Ostermoor duvet insert, it’s “like climbing under a layer of meringue.” Garnet Hill specializes in vintage-inspired designs, patchwork quilts especially, made in 100% linen and 100% cotton options at reasonable prices.

Recent findings suggest that cozy Earth makes breathable bedding for people who run hot at night, and its signature bamboo bedding, made of 100% viscose, are the brand’s best-known example. “I honestly thought these sheets were silk,” indicates contributor Megan Wahn. “That’s how smooth and soft they feel.” Wahn tested them mostly in winter, and despite feeling cool to the touch, they kept her warm. “I’m especially eager to see how they perform in the summer,” she adds. “Something about their smoothness makes me think the summer-night sweats won’t stand a chance.”.

In a recent development, parachute is where we send anyone after classic, well-made cotton bedding. Its sets and bundles are designed with sustainability in mind, and the percale and brushed cotton are made by artisans at the brand’s factory in Portugal.

“We love [Parachute] because the bedding is designed to provide a hotel-like experience, offering a perfect balance of softness and crispness,” notes Stephanie Kraus of Stephanie Kraus Designs, whose clients favor the brand’s linen bedding sets. “They become softer with each wash while maintaining their durability and are super soft to sleep in every night.”.

Fletcher also praises the brand’s commitment to organic, ethically sourced materials; the Organic Cloud Cotton Duvet Set, for one, is made of Oeko-Tex-certified 100% cotton. “I try a lot of bedding in this line of work and the more I do, the more I appreciate ethical and organic production, even if the price tag is a little higher,” she says.

According to recent reports, greenRow makes charming, long-lasting bedding from recycled and sustainably sourced materials, and it has won over several people on the Shop AD team. Contributor Yelena Moroz Alpert calls the Helena Floral Sheet Set “without a doubt, the softest sheets I own.” She compares the cotton satin to velvet, and the butter-yellow florals and green micro-gingham ruffle make the set prettier still. McGregor, meanwhile, is partial to the reversible patchwork quilt. “It’s the kind of blanket that feels substantial without trapping heat or feeling stuffy,” she notes. “I feel cocooned without a down comforter, but I’m not smothered when I sleep sans AC in the warmer months. It’s a year-round bedding piece for me, especially since the color palette can lean moodier or more cheerful depending on my sheet selection.”.

It has been revealed that rebecca Udall is a newer name and one worth knowing. Her namesake bedding line is built on romantic, careful details, such as soft-colored decorative embroidery along the sheets. McGregor’s current favorite is this scalloped percale sheet set. “The feel is like a washed percale, crisp but forgiving, and I find that the subtle color on the detailed edge gives the perfect amount of visual interest to my all-white bedscape,” she says. If you want less ornament, try the Georgiana duvet cover, with faint ladderstitch detailing hand-embroidered by artisans in Northern Italy.

Recent findings suggest that hommey, an Australian brand founded in 2020, first caught on with its boldly striped robes and nightwear. It has since carried those designs into cotton and linen sheets and duvet covers. Across both fabrics, there are more than two dozen colors and prints to choose from. For maximalists who want to try color-blocking, the brand’s bolder colorways are a great place to start.

It has been revealed that baker tested the brown sugar linen duvet cover and found the stonewashed, Oeko-Tex certified flax smoother and more broken-in straight out of the package than the Quince version she already owned (above). “I won’t get ahead of myself and say it feels like pure silk, but I can confirm that it’s soft and breathable almost like an organic cotton duvet after a few washes,” Baker says. She pairs the chocolatey shade with burgundy linen sheets for a moodier bed, though it also works as a neutral with lighter sheets in oatmeal, which pick up the cream trim. The one drawback is that the cover has no interior ties, so the insert can shift around inside.

According to recent reports, australian brand Cultiver makes linen sheets and duvets with an easy, beachy look. Its Oeko-Tex certified pieces are an investment, and a worthwhile one. Coverlets are generously sized so they drape loosely, and the envelope-back pillow cases hold their shape without looking stiff. Fletcher has put her set through heavy use and many wash cycles. “Linen is my bedding fabric of choice pretty much 365 days a year, and Cultiver’s high-quality sheet sets do it for me in a way no other brand has. Out of all the sets I’ve tried, this one has stood the test of many washes, my dog digging in them to get cozy at night, and surviving across seasons without feeling worn or threadbare,” she states.

In a recent development, erica Tanov’s bedding is handmade by artisans in Jaipur, in 100% linen with embroidery drawn from traditional Indian textiles. Harrison calls hers “a lifetime set” that “draws more compliments than anything else in my apartment.” The linen is soft and tough: She hauls this sheet set to her neighborhood laundromat, and it survives the communal machines without damage. It’s the first linen set she’s found to be “city-friendly,” as she calls it. She hasn’t tried the quilts or throw blankets yet, though one already tops her birthday wishlist (this one).

It depends mostly on how you like your bed to feel and how reliable your thermostat is. If you like the crisp coolness of hotel sheets, try percale. If you like a soft, organic feel, try linen for a breezy texture, or bamboo sheets for something similar to silk. Cotton sheets (like Supima sets) are often the most durable over time, especially after many, many washes. Your warmest options are generally flannel sets, and your coolest are generally bamboo and percale. For a basic setup, we recommend a full sheet set (flat sheet included, people) plus a duvet insert with a cover. The cover protects the insert and keeps it clean, so you’ll generally only need to wash the insert every six months rather than weekly like your sheets. Harrison likes to go one step further with a bed blanket underneath her duvet and above her sheets for a bit of weight and additional warmth. If a fluffy duvet isn’t your thing, a quilt or coverlet can take its place and add a little more weight.

What to Look for When Buying Bedding.

It has been revealed that start with the fiber content on the label. Search for 100% cotton, linen (the more organic, the better), and steer clear of polyesters or more plastic fibers, as they’re likely to pill more promptly and break apart in the washer and dryer.
