💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that given the ease with which WWE superstar Jade Cargill delivers a pump kick or spinebuster, it’s hard to believe the 34-year-old hasn’t spent her entire life in the ring.
  • The experience of being a team player has come in handy for Jade as she navigates the world of wrestling.
  • Sources indicate that “I can only be as great as my partner,” she tells editors Abigail Cuffey, Amanda Lucci, and Jacqueline Andriakos on the latest episode of The Huddle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that given the ease with which WWE superstar Jade Cargill delivers a pump kick or spinebuster, it’s hard to believe the 34-year-old hasn’t spent her entire life in the ring. But growing up, Jade was obsessed with a different sport: basketball. In college, she was a forward/guard for the Jacksonville University team then went on to play overseas in France.

The experience of being a team player has come in handy for Jade as she navigates the world of wrestling. Sure, it may often look like a one-on-one competition, but Jade indicates that, if anything, it’s more like a dance.

Sources indicate that “I can only be as great as my partner,” she tells editors Abigail Cuffey, Amanda Lucci, and Jacqueline Andriakos on the latest episode of The Huddle. “I can't do this by myself.”.

Sources indicate that despite having been a part of the WWE since 2023, Jade admits she’s still a “rookie” compared to her ‘dance’ partners—the other women in the league, who inspire her every day. “I've been placed in a very amazing environment with women who strive for greatness, and that's what I want to do,” she claims.

As she prepares to lead a five-woman team at Survivor Series: WarGames on November 28, Jade talks about her unconventional path to wrestling, making peace with mistakes, and the advice she wants every kid watching her to hear.

Jade’s journey to becoming a professional wrestler is the stuff of motivational sports movies. A stay-at-home mom (she took time off work as a child psychologist to raise her daughter), Jade was simply training in the gym to get strong after pregnancy when she was introduced to WWE veteran Mark Henry, who asked if she’d ever considered a career in wrestling.

“I was like, ‘Why not?’” she recalls thinking. “I had a kid and put my life on hold for a little bit. I wanted to do something more. I was like, ‘This body is not done.’ [I] went to a tryout, had no experience at all.”.

Sources indicate that jade left that tryout bruised and battered—and determined to improve. And so she trained and trained and trained some more. She couldn’t get enough. “I just loved it,” she claims. “It's athletics, yes, but also it's improvising, but also it's acting, but also it's your natural instinct. It’s all these things wrapped into one that I just didn't want to put down.”.

All that work eventually paid off: Jade made her professional wrestling debut with All Elite Wrestling in 2020 and then joined the WWE three years later.

Despite all the training and preparation that goes into a match, Jade admits that not a single one has been “perfect.” But in the case where she stumbles off the ropes or throws a lousy punch, Jade simply follows the old maxim, the show must go on.

Recent findings suggest that “I just kind of have the mindset that these things happen,” she claims. “If you do have a mishap, you can't sell it—[the audience doesn’t] know what's going on. You just got to keep going with the punches.”.

Jade also gives a lot of credit to her fellow competitors, who often pick her up—if not physically, then emotionally—after a match, letting her know she’s not alone.

Industry observers note that “I remember my coworker Naomi sent me a clip of her falling, and she was like, ‘Just to show you...’ And I was like, ‘Okay, all right. It happens,’” Jade says. “You’ve just got to keep on going and make your next match the best match.”.

It has been revealed that as a mom, Jade knows how powerful an adult’s example can be—whether it’s a parent’s or a performer’s. Ultimately, she hopes kids are inspired by her hard work and determination, both in and out of the ring, and if they can take away any message, it would be this: “Don't let anyone tell you who you are,” she notes. “Don't let society put you in a box. Go out there and take on the world.”.

And when a new opportunity presents itself, don’t be afraid to give it a try. “If you would have told me five years ago, I would be wrestling. I would have laughed,” she claims. “And look at me now.”.

To hear more from Jade—including her no-frills recovery program—click play on the latest episode of The Huddle above.

Volkswagen is delaying another EV based on the SSP

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After delaying development of the long-awaited electric Golf, Volkswagen is delaying another EV based on its SSP platform.
  • As it scrambles to cut costs, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer revealed in an internal memo at the end of October that development of the all-electric Golf is being delayed at its Wolfsburg plant in Germany.
  • The news comes after the VW Group posted an operating loss of €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its largest quarterly loss since the infamous Dieselgate scandal in 2015.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After delaying development of the long-awaited electric Golf, Volkswagen is delaying another EV based on its SSP platform.

As it scrambles to cut costs, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer revealed in an internal memo at the end of October that development of the all-electric Golf is being delayed at its Wolfsburg plant in Germany.

The news comes after the VW Group posted an operating loss of €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its largest quarterly loss since the infamous Dieselgate scandal in 2015.

Sources indicate that “We simply can’t afford this work right now,” Schäfer stated in the memo reviewed by Reuters. The Wolfsburg plant, AKA the “heart of the VW brand,” is about €300 million ($334.5 million) short of its cost-cutting targets, the memo said.

Volkswagen initially planned to launch the Golf EV in 2028, but Schäfer announced earlier this year that the long-awaited electric car was delayed until closer to 2030.

Schäfer suggested the delay was because the SSP (Scalable Systems Platform), which is being developed through its partnership with Rivian, was taking longer than expected, again due to costs.

According to Autocar, Volkswagen is now delaying the Audi A4 E-tron as well, another vehicle that was initially planned to be among the first based on the SSP platform.

Production of the electric A4 is being pushed back until at least 2029, a year later than originally planned. While the delay is disappointing for Audi fans (including myself) still waiting for an electric A4, it also puts Audi behind rival luxury brands in the mid-size sedan segment.

BMW has the upcoming i3, and Mercedes-Benz has the C-Class EV, both of which feature major improvements in range, charging, and efficiency over their previous-generation EVs.

Volkswagen remarked in 2023 that the 800V SSP will serve as a “single future backbone with integrated electric and electronics architecture,” claiming that more than 40 million models were expected to be built on it.

The company also said investment and R&D costs were expected to be reduced by about 30% compared to the current MEB platform, enabling most models “to achieve the same margin compared to their conventionally powered counterparts.”.

Volkswagen’s software struggles started in its internal division, Cariad, leading to delays, missed targets, and budget overruns.

To fix it, VW turned to Rivian, forming a joint venture to develop its next-gen software-defined vehicle (SDV) electrical architecture.

In March, VW remarked several test vehicles, including the ID.EVERY1, Audi, and Scout with the SDV architecture underwent “comprehensive evaluation,” and successfully validated over-the-air (OTA) functionality.

Being cash efficient is good, but delays to the next-gen platform that will keep you competitive with rival brands seem like a problem.

However, the Audi A4 E-tron delay is not entirely about software. The Autocar report claims Audi demanded significant changes to the SSP platform for the A4 E-tron so it more closely matched the current gas version.

Audi reportedly wanted individual footwells for front and rear passengers, which would require repositioning the battery.

The luxury brand also reportedly asked for a 48V electrical system instead of the traditional 12V setup initially planned.

It has been revealed that while development of the Golf EV is on hold, VW’s works council mentioned the pause will not delay its launch, promising to make up for lost time. It’s still expected to launch in 2030. The Audi A4 E-tron is now expected to arrive around 2029.

#190116. Why So Many New Moms Are Told to Wait to Exercise Again—and What the Research Really Says

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1896 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

Why So Many New Moms Are Told to Wait to Exercise Again—and What the Research Really Says

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1896 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, earlier this year, trainer and WH advisory board member Sohee Carpenter, CSCS, posted an Instagram Reel challenging some conventional postpartum advice: Don’t work out until your ob-gyn clears you at your six-week follow-up appointment.
  • “I feel like so many people get angry because they assume we mean you're going to be doing a one-rep max back squat a week after you have a baby,” Carpenter claims.
  • According to recent reports, the problem, Carpenter explains, is that the six-week rule isn’t based on evidence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, earlier this year, trainer and WH advisory board member Sohee Carpenter, CSCS, posted an Instagram Reel challenging some conventional postpartum advice: Don’t work out until your ob-gyn clears you at your six-week follow-up appointment. Her point wasn’t that upcoming moms should rush back to the gym. It was that one timeline can’t fit everyone. Some women are ready to move sooner, and others need more time.

The Reel ruffled some feathers.

“I feel like so many people get angry because they assume we mean you're going to be doing a one-rep max back squat a week after you have a baby,” Carpenter claims. “But that's definitely not what we're saying.” (By “we,” she means trainers who keep up with the latest research on pregnancy and postpartum exercise.).

According to recent reports, the problem, Carpenter explains, is that the six-week rule isn’t based on evidence. On the contrary, research suggests that this type of blanket advice doesn’t make sense for something as personal as postpartum recovery. When you return to exercise after childbirth should depend on your own symptoms, not a date on the calendar.

“There's really nothing magical about the six-week time point,” indicates Margie Davenport, PhD, a professor of kinesiology at the University of Alberta and chair of the 2025 Canadian Guidelines for Physical Activity for Pregnancy and Postpartum—the first-ever exercise guidelines to specifically focus on evidence-based suggestions for that first year postpartum. In the U.S., the main guidance from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) covers pregnancy and the postpartum period together. ACOG’s guidance points in the same direction, though: It says many women can start exercising again within days of an uncomplicated birth. In fact, “there is no identified ideal time to return,” Davenport says.

Based on the wide range of comments on Carpenter’s post—some supportive, some hypercritical, and still others asking more questions to try to better understand this shift away from the advice they’ve always heard—there’s still a lot of confusion around postpartum exercise. So we asked experts to break down what the research actually notes, and how to approach working out in this new chapter of life.

According to recent reports, in many cultures, the first 30 or 40 days postpartum is traditionally considered a protected time to rest, relax, and recover, Davenport notes. In Chinese culture, it’s called zuo yuezi, which translates to “sitting the month.” In many Latin American and Latino communities, it’s known as “la cuarentena,” a nod to its roughly 40-day length. In South Korea, it’s sanhujori, or “postpartum care.”.

These traditions carry deep cultural significance and are meant to offer real healing and support after birth from one’s community (they put “it takes a village” into practice). They’re rooted in caregiving and cultural custom, and they were never meant to serve as a medical timeline for when it’s safe to start exercising.

In Western medicine, six weeks has become an important medical benchmark in postpartum recovery—and, over time, a default point for returning to exercise too. “At that point, your uterus should be back to its pre-pregnancy state, and so a lot of the gynecologic changes should be fairly reversed by that point,” says Rita Deering, DPT, PhD, associate professor of exercise science and director of the Pelvic Health, Exercise & Musculoskeletal (PHEM) Research Laboratory at Marquette University.

In a recent development, the first six weeks after birth are also when the risk of complications like high blood pressure and infection is highest, Deering notes, which is part of why that window became an key medical checkpoint (even though some pregnancy-related changes take longer to resolve). But, she says, “it was never intended to be about exercise.”.

So how did six weeks become the exercise rule? Before researchers knew much about how safe it is to exercise during pregnancy and after birth, working out was considered potentially risky, Deering notes. There wasn’t strong evidence that exercise wouldn’t slow healing or raise the odds of complications. So the most cautious advice was simply to wait until a doctor confirmed you’d healed enough to resume physical activity.

Sources indicate that to come up with the 2025 Canadian Guidelines, researchers did a deep dive of all the available research on the topic, which included 574 unique studies organized into seven systematic reviews based on 21 different outcomes of postpartum exercise—such as depression and anxiety, low-back pain, injuries, glucose and blood pressure levels, and more. They also assembled an international panel of experts to give their recommendations.

Their advice: Start light-intensity physical activity and mobilization (think: carrying your baby around your home, a slow walk down the block, pelvic floor physical therapy) right away. From there, progress as you feel ready to moderate-to-vigorous activity such as brisk walking, resistance training, and running at your own pace—as long as tears and incisions have sufficiently healed and you don’t experience additional bleeding with exercise. (As mentioned, ACOG similarly recommends that women can return to postnatal exercise within days after an uncomplicated birth.).

Recent findings suggest that based on the research, there are no “absolute contraindications” to exercise postpartum, Davenport states—meaning no condition would rule out exercise entirely. There are some relative contraindications, she explains, “where you might have to delay a little bit or modify the type of activity that you're doing.” Examples include severe abdominal pain, extreme fatigue, and C-section incision pain that worsens with activity. All warrant a conversation with your doctor before starting.

Want to Know More About Lifting While Pregnant? Start Here.

It has been revealed that pelvic floor symptoms, like leaking urine or a feeling of heaviness in the vagina, aren’t a reason to stop exercising altogether. If you notice signs of pelvic floor dysfunction, the guidelines recommend starting slowly and building up gradually instead. “Some leakage is okay,” Davenport indicates. “It means that the training that you’re doing is just overloading the muscle.”.

Many people, including plenty of commenters on Carpenter’s Reel, worry that exercising after birth will damage the pelvic floor and cause dysfunction. But the evidence doesn’t support that. In fact, those muscles will likely be better off if you resume training, especially if you do exercises to target them in particular. “Engaging in pelvic floor muscle training reduces your risk of urinary incontinence by around 37 percent,” Davenport indicates. Additionally, if you stop all exercise because you're leaking a little bit, “this can actually mean that you're missing out on those other benefits.”.

One caveat: If you’re leaking a lot, or it’s getting worse over time, “you probably need to pull it back,” Davenport notes. That means being more selective about the moves you choose. For example, you might skip long runs and high-impact moves like jump squats for now, adds Sheridan Skye, a registered nurse, pre- and postnatal fitness coach, and founder of The Female Fitness Formula. Stick with lower-impact exercises, then build up gradually as you get stronger and your symptoms level off or improve.

Industry observers note that at the end of the day, every body, birth, and recovery is vastly different. “Some people have a very uncomplicated labor and delivery and pregnancy; for others, it's quite complex,” says Davenport. “It only makes sense that the way that they're returning and what time they're actually returning is also going to be quite individualized.”.

Recent findings suggest that for some fresh moms, six weeks is too soon, and a blanket deadline only adds stress. “Maybe they aren't sleeping or they don't have the support to be able to return [to exercise] at six weeks,” Davenport says. On the flip side, for someone who had a straightforward delivery and is itching to get moving again, “telling them to wait for six weeks with no evidence to support it is also inappropriate.”.

It has been revealed that in fact, exercise can offer significant benefits during postpartum recovery, even before the six-week mark. “It improves muscle and bone density that we lose throughout pregnancy,” Skye indicates. Postpartum exercise is associated with a 45 percent reduction in the odds of developing postpartum depression, and starting before 12 weeks is even more beneficial.

It’s also associated with a 28 percent reduction in the risk of developing diabetes postpartum. Exercise even improves sleep quality, Skye notes. “Women tend to feel more energized and like they've experienced more rest, even if they haven't,” she says. (Anyone who’s survived a 3 a.m. feeding stretch knows that’s no small thing!).

There is also evidence that exercise in general can help to decrease pain, claims Deering, and research links sedentary behavior to lumbopelvic (the areas of the lower back and pelvis) pain. “So if you are having pain, movement might be what you need to help with that.”.

For many people, it may be difficult to know if you’re truly ready. “Especially when you're postpartum, it can feel like you are super out of touch with your body sensations, especially if you're not sleeping well,” Carpenter states.

If you're at the point where you're thinking about it, but are nervous or unsure or just overwhelmed by having another decision to make, Davenport recommends taking the Get Active Questionnaire for Postpartum—a tool that her team designed as part of the 2025 guideline. It can help you rapidly understand if you’re ready to start from a medical perspective. That can help give you some reassurance.

According to recent reports, there can also be “a lot of fear involved,” Carpenter says, especially if you had a C-section or are healing from a vaginal tear. In that case, “you’re probably going to be a bit hesitant,” which is completely understandable. Starting slower and lighter than you think you need to is perfectly fine as you get reacquainted with your body. “The first several sessions are really about mentally trying to get that confidence back,” she says.

As you go, pay attention to how your body responds. Leaking, for instance? That’s not a reason to stop exercising, but you may want to adjust your workout to reduce it. More bleeding, new pain, or a sense that something just doesn’t feel right are signs to stop, reassess, and possibly scale back. If they don’t improve, check in with your doctor. “It’s really about setting your ego aside and being willing to modify, even if it’s one rep to the next, based on how you’re feeling right at that time,” Carpenter says.

Recent findings suggest that and if you feel physically ready but aren’t quite there mentally? “It’s okay to honor those feelings,” Deering says, “and to recognize that it’s okay to give yourself some time.” Whether that’s two weeks, six weeks, or six months, the right moment to start moving is the one that works for you.

Amy is a freelance writer and editor who covers health, fitness, and lifestyle topics—with a focus on practical advice that fits into real life. She previously worked as deputy fitness editor at SELF, and is both an ACE-certified personal trainer and a ProNatal pre and postnatal fitness specialist. Her work has been published in Women’s Health, Men’s Health, SELF, Wondermind, HGTV, Outside, REAL SIMPLE, The Fresh York Times for Kids, and more. Amy lives in central New York where she spends her off-hours chasing after her two kids, digging into backyard gardening projects with her husband, and creatively squeezing at-home workouts into her schedule as often as she can.

BYD’s new flagship Tang SUV starts at about $34,000 with two enormous screens

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (623 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • BYD opened pre-orders for the third-generation Tang starting at about $34,000 in China.
  • The third-generation Tang joins the Great Tang, or Da Tang, as it’s called in China in BYD’s expanding flagship SUV lineup.
  • We knew it was coming soon after the latest model appeared in a regulatory filing in China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) last month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD opened pre-orders for the third-generation Tang starting at about $34,000 in China. This five-seat flagship SUV packs more than you’d expect for the money, with two massive 30-inch-plus screens inside and up to 850 km (528 miles) of CLTC range.

The third-generation Tang joins the Great Tang, or Da Tang, as it’s called in China in BYD’s expanding flagship SUV lineup.

We knew it was coming soon after the latest model appeared in a regulatory filing in China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) last month.

BYD announced on Friday that pre-orders for the third-gen Tang are officially open, starting at 225,000 yuan, which is around $34,000.

The “large five-seat flagship SUV,” as BYD calls it, is available in three variants, priced from 225,000 yuan ($34,000), 240,000 yuan ($36,000), and 260,000 yuan ($39,000) with rear- and all-wheel-drive variants.

The two lower-priced variants are both RWD, offering a CLTC range of up to 850 km (528 miles), while the top-spec dual-motor AWD version has up to 770 km (478 miles).

All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging tech, enabling the battery to be charged from 10% to 80% in five minutes, or nine minutes to go from 10% to 97%.

Inside, the five-seat SUV packs a surprising amount of tech and premium extras for the price. The setup features two massive screens: a 35.4″ integrated display and another 30″ panoramic theater screen.

Unlike its predessor, which offered five and six-seat configurations, the third-gen Tang will only be offered as a five-seater.

The five-seat setup opens up interior space for passengers and the third-gen Tang has the largest front trunk (frunk) in its class at 205L, BYD stated.

Like many of its newly introduced flagship vehicles, the third-gen Tang is equipped with BYD’s latest tech, including its God’s Eye B driver-assistance system and Disus-A dual-chamber intelligent air suspension body control system.

Other added features include a 22-speaker Dynaudio sound system, intelligent electric all‑wheel drive, a high-speed tire blowout stability system, and its iTAC intelligent torque control system.

Lu Tian, the general manager of BYD’s Dynasty division mentioned third-gen Tang vehicles have arrived at dealerships nationwide.

Industry observers note that why mention "two enormous screens" like they are some markers of a more premium vehicle or represent some value? We don't measure the utility of cars by screen real estate per dollar. It's the other part of the utility that matter: range, driving dynamics, road trip convenience, fit/finish/materials/insulation. Personally, I don't think "enormous screens" are going to age well as an automotive trend.

The Great Tang received over 150,000 preorders by the time it launched in mid-June, a record for a single BYD model.

Since its official launch, the larger Great Tang (Da Tang) has sold more than 10,000 units for four straight months now.

It has been revealed that the Great Tang is on sale in China in pure electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains. The cheapest EV variant starts at 239,900 yuan ($35,500) a CLTC driving range of 800 km (497 miles). 💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that volkswagen is getting ready to launch a fresh electric car starting at about €20,000 ($22,000) in 2027, and it looks like the entry-level EV may no longer be nameless.
  • Industry observers note that the new entry-level EV is “the last piece of the puzzle,” Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer mentioned last March after unveiling the ID.
  • Volkswagen said the production version will launch in 2027 with a starting price of around €20,000 ($22,000).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that volkswagen is getting ready to launch a fresh electric car starting at about €20,000 ($22,000) in 2027, and it looks like the entry-level EV may no longer be nameless. A newly filed trademark could have just given away what VW looks to call it.

Industry observers note that the new entry-level EV is “the last piece of the puzzle,” Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer mentioned last March after unveiling the ID. EVERY1 concept car.

Volkswagen said the production version will launch in 2027 with a starting price of around €20,000 ($22,000).

Sources indicate that the newly introduced model will sit below the ID. Polo in Volkswagen’s Electric Urban Car Family, a lineup of compact, affordable electric cars.

According to recent reports, volkswagen’s current entry-level EV lineup includes the ID. Polo, ID. Cross, the Cupra Raval, and Skoda Epiq, all based on its new MEB+ platform.

After launching the lower-priced standard versions of the ID. Polo and ID. Cross recently, starting at €24,995 and €27,995, respectively, Volkswagen is preparing to launch an even smaller, more affordable EV next year.

A recent trademark filing with the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) and the German DPMA may have just revealed the name of VW’s upcoming €20,000 EV.

In a recent development, volkswagen filed a trademark application for the name ID. UP on October 22, 2026, with the EUIPO and DPMA, suggesting this will be the name of the upcoming electric car in 2027.

The trademark follows previous reports that VW planned to revive the former Up! name as part of its shift away from its previous numerical naming scheme (ID.3, ID.4, ID.5, etc.).

In a recent development, volkswagen has kept most details a secret thus far. Like the ID. Polo, the first to go on sale with an established VW nameplate, the ID. UP is expected to use the same 37 kWh LFP battery to reduce costs.

It has been revealed that the VW ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery offers a WLTP range of up to 334 km (207 miles), so the smaller ID. UP will likely provide around the same, if not slightly more.

Volkswagen said it will offer at least 250 km (155 miles) of range. It will also use a upcoming 70 kW (94 hp) electric motor, enabling a top speed of 130 km/h (80 mph).

It has been revealed that the production version of the ID. EVERY1, expected to arrive as the ID. UP, will be one of nine new models VW looks to launch by 2027.

Volkswagen previously noted the entry-level EV will be 3,880 mm long, which would position it between the former Up! (3,600 mm) and the ID. Polo (4,053 mm). Despite its compact size, VW said the electric city car will seat four passengers and offer a luggage compartment volume of 305 liters.

The VW Group’s new Electric Urban Car Family is off to a strong start, securing nearly 150,000 orders after series production began in June.

All models within the family are built on the MEB+ platform with a FWD powertrain, and share more than 80% of the components and tech.

Volkswagen noted the production version of the ID. EVERY1 will be among the first vehicles based on its zonal, software-defined vehicle (SDV) architecture, which it is developing through its joint venture with Rivian.

Ah, finally a car in the upper range of being meaningful and sensible.

Recent findings suggest that if someone needs more, then those are obviously special needs people. Being like can't enter and exit such a sensible car. Or like having to move the 15 horses of their 5 daughters. Or being a fieldworker driving a gazillion miles every day. Or requiring a lot of attention from lesser beings.

In March, the Rivian and Volkswagen Group Technologies (RV Tech) joint venture tested the latest SDV architecture on the ID. EVERY1, alongside Audi and Scout reference vehicles, validating over-the-air (OTA) capabilities.

The newly introduced architecture will enable “highly automated driving features” and “advanced infotainment solutions,” with continuous OTA updates.

While VW noted it will deploy the SDV architecture in “electric vehicles across markets in the Western Hemisphere,” the entry-level EV is not expected to reach the States.

In a recent development, volkswagen is, however, preparing to launch the ID. Tiguan, which will launch in 2027 as the successor to the ID.4 (and ID.5 in Europe).

According to recent reports, the Smartwool Active Mesh Short Sleeve was hands-down the best moisture-wicking shirt we tested over the past few months—and for good reason. Recent findings suggest that one of my favorite things about this shirt is how well it hides sweat. I wore it during a tough HIIT session, and there were zero visible sweat stains, no matter which color I had on (and yes, I tried all three). That’s thanks to the merino wool, which is blended with Tencel Lyocell—a soft, breathable fabric made from wood pulp that helps regulate temperature and manage moisture like a pro.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve put this shirt through the wringer—running, yoga, lifting, HIIT—and it always holds up. It never feels clingy, gives you room to move without any added bulk, and has reflective elements for better visibility during late-night runs.

Another major plus: the waist-length cut offers great coverage, so you don’t have to worry about it riding up when you’re bending, stretching, or running. It doesn’t come with built-in support, so just pair it with your favorite sports bra and you’re good to go.

The Lululemon Ebb to Street Tank is a reliable favorite among WH editors. It’s super soft, seamless, sweat-wicking, and ultra stretchy thanks to a comfortable blend of elastane and nylon. This is one of my go-to tops for working out or running errands. However, you should note that because there are no adjustable straps, you can't customize the fit of this tank.

And, we found that it actually does keep us feeling covered and protected during low-impact exercise, which we didn’t find to be the case with other tanks that have built-in bras.

Another pro? The longer length of this top (it hits at the hip) keeps us feeling locked in and covered during workouts where we don’t want a ton of stomach showing.

Recent findings suggest that while it does a great job at keeping us dry during sweaty workouts, we found that, in terms of support, it’s not the best choice for high-intensity training. It didn’t do a great job of holding the girls in place during high-impact moves, and we would have liked more padding and compression. But based on our testing, it's difficult to find a tank with that level of support. That's why we recommend pairing this with our favorite high-impact sports bra, the Under Armour Infinity 2.0 High Sports Bra.

The fabric of your moisture-wicking top can either help or hinder sweat management, so you want to make sure you're investing in materials with sweat-wicking technology that can hold up through multiple washes.

Most technical fabrics have specific washing and drying instructions, and if you want to maximize your workout wardrobe’s function and durability, it’s a good idea to follow those instructions to the letter. Pay special attention to the temperature of the water the instructions call for, whether or not the items can be placed in the dryer and at what temp they can be dried, or whether line drying is advised.

WH fitness and reviews editor Natascha Grief, NASM-CPT opts for line drying and avoids the dryer altogether when possible for any kind of technical fabric; when that’s not an option, she always sets the dryer at the lowest temperature possible.

Sources indicate that SLING BAGS ARE here to stay, gentlemen, and to be honest, they’re a lighter and smarter way to commute with your EDC when backpacks and duffel bags feel like overkill. Worn across the body (unlike a fanny pack, which is designed to sit around the waist), sling bags are easy to carry, super practical, and able to transport all your daily essentials using a bunch of accessible compartments, zippers, and pockets. The best sling bags for men offer a range of styles for every kind of guy, whether you’re commuting, traveling, or heading into the outdoors. Some are minimal and sleek, while others favor the rugged and technical.

Industry observers note that if you’re stuck on which sling bag to pick, don’t sweat it—our team tested and narrowed down the top contenders. Below, we’ve included 11 standout picks that combine comfort, style, and hands-free functionality from notable brands like Peak Design, Lululemon, and The North Face.

In a recent development, we gave 20 different sling bags a test run, but Lululemon’s offering takes the cake. The Everywhere Belt Bag is all about making things easier for the man on the go. For starters, you can throw it over your shoulder or wear it around your waist like a fanny pack for when you're on the trail or at an outdoor concert (or any other time you want to be hands-free). The main pouch features a double two-way zipper that opens three-quarters of the way, letting you see and reach everything inside without having to dig around blindly. Another bonus: There’s a smaller pocket tucked into the back with a single zipper, which makes it ideal for hiding cash, cards, and other small valuables.

Thanks to the water-resistant nylon exterior, anything stowed away will remain dry, in the event it starts pouring rain. Our favorite part, however, is the strap that we found to be one of the most comfortable ones that we’ve tested. As for the colorway, you can choose from a bunch of neutral tones, but our fashion team recommends going with the eucalyptus hue—you’re bound to be the center of attention.

Sources indicate that while it can’t store a water bottle, we love how effortlessly our gadgets and snacks fit inside. Not to mention, it has so much versatility in regard to style. You can wear it with your best sweatsuit or casual fit and look fly for the day’s festivities.

Read More: Best Fanny Packs for Men.

Recent findings suggest that this Amazon best-seller is spot-on for your next adventure. It’s really got organization in spades with mesh pockets on two sides for bottles or umbrellas, a small front zipper pocket for smaller devices, and a massive space inside that’s designed like a backpack. It’s smartly compartmentalized into smaller sections for anything from keys, passports, snacks, and other bits and bobs. During a camping trip, we made use of the main pocket inside, which is big enough to store your phone and tablet, a feature that we deemed essential in a travel sling bag.

Sources indicate that you can even enjoy your music on your commute as the convenient opening on the front provides easy access to your earphones. It comes in every color imaginable, but the teal blue and reflective details will help you stand out and offer nighttime visibility. And unlike others in this guide, this one comes with a water bottle holder, so you stay hydrated on the move.

Read More: Best Backpacks for Men.

As one of the smaller sling bags in our guide, the Topo Designs Mini Quick Pack has substantial storage where it matters most. We found that its capacity is perfect for shorter trips and daily errands, and the straps are a piece of cake to adjust (though there are quite a few straps). Whenever we don’t need a huge backpack and want to pack light, this little guy is a star.

Sources indicate that in our experience, we’ve worn it on the waist and across the body. One tester was able to utilize the bike light attachment loop for a nighttime ride to increase visibility. And with a solid amount of space and interior organization for a phone, cardholder, and other odds and ends, our editors have also tucked it under a thin coat when we’re in a tight spot. Plus, the unique color-blocked design earns it some extra style points.

While we still feel it works great for the city, this ruggedly built sling is perfect for outdoor adventurists. Firstly, it’s offered in two different sizes with a 6- or 9-liter size, ensuring that if you need a little extra space, you can spend an extra $10 to upgrade. Even in the smaller size, you can easily fit a water bottle plus all of your other gear like earbuds, sunglasses, phone, EDC essentials, protein bar, plus more thanks to the expandable gusset.

One of the cool features of this bag that you won’t find on others is that it comes with sturdy quick-release buckles on both sides, making it ideal no matter which shoulder you toss it around. It offers various storage compartments, 10 to be exact, even with a soft-lined pouch that is great for your phone or sunglasses, helping to avoid scratching while on the move—plus, the padded back and bottom help to protect everything else. Its water resistance and six-year warranty make it the perfect outdoor bag.

It has been revealed that the North Face’s Base Camp Voyager Sling is basically a mini backpack in disguise that’s built to take a beating. This thing held up through packed subways, bike rides, and overhead bin shoves without a single scuff. The shell’s made from abrasion-resistant polyester fabric, the same ultra-tough material as the brand’s duffels, which are designed for actual expeditions, so your daily commute? No sweat.

There’s a padded sleeve that snugly fits a tablet, reflective accents for low-light visibility (great for late-night rides), and a thick, padded shoulder strap that’s actually comfortable to wear all day. Bonus: There’s a zip pocket on the strap that perfectly fits your phone, so no more digging around at crosswalks.

We also loved how the design leans more toward a backpack than a bag. It’s minimalist, structured, and doesn’t flop around when you’re on the move. Whether you’re weaving through downtown foot traffic or navigating an airport terminal, this is the kind of sling that keeps up, and doesn’t look out of place when you stop for a coffee.

If you’re looking for a more elevated sling, then you’ll definitely want to grab this leather Blake Belt Bag from Leatherology. We recommend opting for the standard-size model, as it holds about 5 liters, but it also comes in slim and mini models. You can choose from 10 colors, including three in smooth full-grain, six in pebbled full-grain, a black croc leather, and a groovy fairway green color (very reminiscent of The Masters’ signature color).

The adjustable strap is quite versatile, with the options of wearing it as a traditional crossbody bag, hanging off one shoulder, or around the waist, though, as it’s a unisex model, the strap may be just a touch too short for some guys. That said, it can hold a good amount of gear with its main zippered compartment, which comes with four interior card slots and a decent-sized interior mesh pocket that is also zippered. While some note that the zippers are a little stiff, over time they do tend to wear in and work much easier. Plus, for an additional fee, you can personalize it to truly make it one of a kind.

Eddie Bauer’s Mini Crossbody Bag proves that you don’t have to spend significant to get a reliable everyday carry. Made from nylon, this compact bag punches above its weight when it comes to utility. During testing, we found the slightly 0.8L capacity to be just right. It’s big enough to fit your phone, wallet, keys, and a lip balm, but small enough to stay light and nimble when you’re clocking your daily step count goal. I love the front cargo pocket that has a flap closure. It kept essentials like subway cards or AirPods secure but easy to access when we were on the go.

Sources indicate that yeah, it’s too small to carry a tablet or water bottle, but it comes in clutch for light carry days and quick errands. One tester wore it on a weekend trip and appreciated how easy it was to sling over a jacket without ever feeling bulky. The strap adjusts smoothly and stays comfortable during hours of walking, and after a few days of use, the bag still looked good as new.

Reigning Champ’s crossbody bag is reliable for outdoor gear because it combines smart construction and water-resistant materials. This resilient twill bag is the practical choice to go anywhere, and though it may look compact, there’s plenty of space and interior pockets to keep your stuff organized without looking overloaded. I even wore this during a rainy evening commute, and everything inside, from my phone to loose bills, stayed bone dry.

The adjustable webbing strap is quite comfortable, even if you plan on wearing it all day long. With it, you get two main zippered pockets, plus an internal zippered pocket, and you even get a small front-facing zippered pocket for quick access when you need it. Though it only comes in one color, there’s really not a more versatile accessory color than black, anyway. And it looks darn good with a slight pop of white in its logo.

We love a bag that comes in more than one size, and the Everyday Sling from Peak Design comes in three different sizes: 3-, 6-, and 10-liter options, making it one of the most versatile choices available. Not only that, but it’s also available in seven different colors, ensuring that whatever your taste is, there is definitely a pick for you. Another thing that we really like about this bag is the ability to loosen (or tighten) the quick-adjuster and padded straps while still wearing it.

While this bag is designed with creatives in mind to be able to hold all of your tech, like cameras, laptops (depending on size choice), lenses, rangefinders, and more (thanks to its comfy and padded design), it can still be a great option to use hiking or biking with its weatherproof design and 400D shell construction. While it is resistant to the elements, some reviewers do mention to be cautious with heavier rainfall, though the majority note it can handle most situations.

Traveling around the city, either to and from work, running errands, or just heading to the local coffee shop means finding a bag that’s just big enough to hold the essentials, yet one that’s not gonna weigh you down. Aer’s City Sling 2 is the perfectly sized bag for city activities and commuting. It weighs under a pound and holds 2.5 liters, which means you can still get all of your EDC gear in there with ease.

It has been revealed that even though it’s lightweight, it’s darn tough with its 700D Cordura nylon design and aircraft-grade aluminum tension locks, which means you don’t sacrifice durability. It has a quick-access front pocket for things like keychains, while its back zippered pocket is better for valuables like passports or wallets, with ample room in its main zippered compartment, too. Plus, its strap hides away thanks to its magnetic fastener, converting it into a mobile dopp kit in a pinch. While the strap is tough, it may be a little rough on the shoulder after a day of wear.

According to recent reports, oakley’s Extractor Sling is basically a backpack in disguise, making it perfect for work commutes. It has the capacity to serve as one with several compartments and pockets to transport goods like your hand cream, portable charger, and office laptop. We found this sling bag specifically useful for when we want to pack more without overdoing it.

Industry observers note that you can even fit your gym shorts and workout shirts inside to hit a quick session once you’re off the clock. Plus, the back panel is equipped with air channels to help deliver more breathability and comfort while you’re on the move. Although the downside is that it is heavier than others we’ve tested, it’s got the volume you need to load it all in.

Industry observers note that the best sling bags for men should offer features that cater to your needs. Typically smaller than a messenger bag, they can be worn across the body, over a shoulder, or even around the waist. The sling bags in our guide range from 1.5 liters of capacity to 30 liters.

In a recent development, when looking for one, consider the layout and accessibility of the compartments, pockets, and dedicated spaces for laptops, smartphones, tablets, or water bottles. All in all, there should be ample storage capacity (usually measured and listed in liters) that allows for smart organization and easy reach.

Since sling bags are often worn over one shoulder or across the body, the best sling bags for men need to have adjustable straps and padding to distribute weight evenly across your shoulders and back—a properly fitted sling bag should feel comfortable and not strain you even when worn for extended periods. Therefore, pay attention to the strap’s material, width, and adjustability.

A lightweight sling bag is usually better since it is easier to carry and feels better on your body by preventing unnecessary strain on your shoulders and back, especially if you initiative to use the sling bag for hours on end, or carry it while hiking. Ultimately, the weight of a sling bag will depend on the bag's capacity, design, and intended uses.

To find the best sling bags for men, myself and Joseph Cheatham, led by our Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower, put them through real-life situations. We loaded them up with our usual gear like our phone, wallet, keys, snacks, even a water bottle to see how they handle the weight. The ones we tested have been worn at outdoor festivals, during day hikes, through long-haul flights, and of course, out and about running weekend errands. We paid close attention to the pockets and zippers, but really made sure to assess how comfortable the adjustable straps lie on our shoulders.

Many sling bags are actually designed to accommodate laptops or tablets. These sling bags usually fall on the larger, more functional side, with a large capacity and spacious interior compartment, as well as dedicated padded compartments or sleeves that offer protection and secure storage for your electronic devices.

Recent findings suggest that sling bags are versatile just like backpacks, hence, with the right style and design, they can work in a variety of places. A sleek, leather option looks professional enough for the office and goes well with your office fits. A rugged, weather-resistant one is great for outdoor activities—in fact, there are sling bags designed for purposes like hiking and traveling. For your casual outings, a small, stylish sling bag will work wonders.

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rinnai has launched a new lineup of electric heat pump water heaters that adds wifi controls and more installation options to an appliance that can cut the energy needed for hot showers.
  • The REHPW series comes in 50-, 65-, and 80-gallon sizes.
  • Industry observers note that heat pump water heaters pull heat from the surrounding air and transfer it into the tank.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rinnai has launched a new lineup of electric heat pump water heaters that adds wifi controls and more installation options to an appliance that can cut the energy needed for hot showers.

The REHPW series comes in 50-, 65-, and 80-gallon sizes. It builds on Rinnai’s existing REHP lineup, with changes designed to make the units easier to install, monitor, and maintain.

Industry observers note that heat pump water heaters pull heat from the surrounding air and transfer it into the tank. Moving that heat requires less electricity than producing it with conventional electric resistance elements. There’s no fuel combustion at the appliance, although emissions from its electricity supply depend on the grid.

Rinnai lists a Uniform Energy Factor, or UEF, of 3.75 for the 50-gallon model and 4.0 for the two larger versions. Higher numbers mean greater efficiency under standardized testing; actual bills depend on electricity rates, hot water use, and installation conditions.

Recent findings suggest that the lineup delivers up to 91 gallons of hot water in the first hour, depending on tank size. That rating includes both stored hot water and what the unit can heat during that hour – useful context when several people take consecutive showers.

It has been revealed that there are five operating modes, 4.5 kW backup heating elements, and a variable-speed fan designed to keep noise down. The heat pump can operate with ambient air as low as 37°F.

Installation is where some of the more practical upgrades show up.

The new Rinnai heat pump water heater units have water connections on both the top and side, giving installers more options for connecting existing plumbing. Both the air intake and exhaust are on top, allowing zero side clearance where Rinnai’s installation requirements permit.

An optional ducting kit adds flexibility for tighter spaces. Carrying handles help with moving the tank into place, and the air filter slides out horizontally from the side for cleaning.

Rinnai has also added a third tank temperature sensor to the 50- and 80-gallon models to help manage hot water delivery.

Wifi adds remote monitoring and control. Rinnai’s updated Central app supports the REHPW series, including scheduling and tools to use time-of-use electricity rates to manage energy use.

Sources indicate that the units also carry CTA-2045 AC Level 2 certification for demand response. That gives compatible utility programs a way to communicate with the water heater and adjust its electricity use. Rinnai claims the certification can help qualify homeowners for local and state utility demand-response rebates; availability depends on the program.

The series is Energy Star certified, meets NEEA Tier 4 requirements, and complies with California’s Title 24 requirements, including JA13, according to Rinnai. Warranty coverage includes 10 years for the tank and other parts, plus one year for labor.

Industry observers note that I’m very happy with my hybrid heat pump water heater. I run it in heat pump only mode in summer and it helps cool the house for free. For anyone on the fence, especially your utility offers a rebate, it’s definitely worth looking at.

Rinnai directs buyers to an installer for pricing, so the upfront cost – and how much a local rebate might offset it – will require a quote. However, the REHP series price on Amazon hovers around the $2,000 mark.

Tesla Cybercab orders open at $29,990 + $299/mo, only in Robotaxi zones

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1043 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”.
  • And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.
  • Tesla’s official Robotaxi account announced the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”.

And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account announced the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.

The order page lists the Cybercab at $29,990 before taxes, with an estimated delivery of December 2026 in Austin, Texas. You need to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit to order.

The subscription isn’t optional. It’s pre-checked on the order page at $299 per month, with one month included, and the fine print states “Subscription and regular vehicle maintenance required to operate.”.

In a recent development, the email is even more direct. Its asterisk reads: “Only available in supported service areas. Subscription required for operation.”.

Industry observers note that the rest is what we already knew. Two seats, a 21-inch center touchscreen, 20.1 cubic feet of cargo space, and no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla calls it “fully autonomous” and claims you’ll “manage your ride in the app.”.

In a recent development, musk had promised a Cybercab “below $30,000” when he unveiled it in 2024. He technically hit it. He just didn’t mention the $3,588 a year it takes to use it. Over five years, that’s about $47,600 for a two-seater, before insurance, maintenance, taxes, and charging.

Tesla runs its Robotaxi service in eight cities: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. That’s where a Cybercab can operate. Everywhere else, it’s a $30,000 sculpture in your driveway.

Sources indicate that and those service areas aren’t what Tesla says they are. Independent tracker Koby Pierce tested thousands of addresses in the Robotaxi app and found that the areas where Tesla actually accepts pickups and drop-offs are only 59% to 78% of the advertised geofences in the six cities he checked. In Austin, the very city where Tesla is delivering these cars, it’s about 59%.

Railroad crossings are a massive reason why. In Houston, the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app quoting about 40 minutes to go two blocks downtown because the vehicle appeared to route around rail crossings. Tesla also lists San Antonio’s airport inside its polygon but doesn’t serve it.

Industry observers note that then there’s the regulatory cloud. NHTSA has ordered Tesla to prove under oath that a car with no brake pedal meets federal safety standards that require one. Tesla answered on October 30 and asked that the entire response be kept confidential. NHTSA hasn’t ruled. Tesla is now selling the car to consumers anyway.

It has been revealed that I think this is going to be a total mess. It looks like Tesla is only doing this by invitation and delivering it in Austin to prove they can deliver an “unsupervised” vehicle in 2026.

Tesla is going to sell these to fans who are excited about owning a self-driving car, and many of them will find out the limitations aren’t worth $299 a month on top of a $30,000 car.

Recent findings suggest that sure, if your monthly Uber bill is well over $300 and you live and work deep inside the geofence, maybe the math works on paper. Until you realize you have to park it somewhere once you get to your destination. Or that it can’t take you to a friend’s place two neighborhoods over. Or that a 15-minute drive turns into an hour because the car won’t cross a train track. With an Uber or a Waymo, that’s someone else’s problem. With a Cybercab, you’re paying for the privilege.

No point trying to calculate what it will cost over X years. Tesla can change that monthly fee at will anyway (and shall be expected to, considering their overall pricing history).

And here’s the part that makes no sense to me. The Cybercab runs on the same AI4 computer as the current Model Y. Tesla already runs unsupervised Model Y Robotaxis in these same geofences. So why can’t the Model Y owners who already paid for “Full Self-Driving” get unsupervised operation in those same zones? Wouldn’t be even easier to turn that on these vehicles which have accumulated much more data? Tesla keeps pushing that to “next year,” currently around Q2 2027, while asking people to buy a newly introduced two-seater that can do nothing else.

It has been revealed that if the tech works unsupervised in Austin, turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin. If it doesn’t, why should anyone pay $47,000 over five years for a car that only works where Tesla says it does?

Like with every other Tesla product lately, the delivered version is going to be a lot more disappointing than the one that was sold on stage.

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, and it works anywhere, no geofence required. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. And with lease and PPA options, you can do it with zero upfront cost and start saving immediately. If you want to find the best deal, check out EnergySage. It’s a free service with hundreds of pre-vetted installers competing for your business, so you save 20 to 30% compared to going it alone. No sales calls until you pick an installer. I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian’s bike

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1072 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging.
  • Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.
  • When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. We’ve already standardized much of our lives around the convenient little connector, from phones and laptops to tablets and countless other gadgets. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.

Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.

When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.

It has been revealed that USB-C charging on electric bikes isn’t entirely newly introduced, but it’s surprisingly rare. Ampler was one of the first companies to introduce it barely a year ago, though its bikes are sadly no longer in production after the organization’s bankruptcy. More recently, Rivian’s ALSO electric bike arrived with USB-C charging, but that bike costs around $4,500 – at least if you want the model that’s slowly starting to ship.

Recent findings suggest that the ENGWE Zip, on the other hand, costs roughly a quarter as much as its only USB-charging competition. At €999, it’s priced at a relatively affordable US$1,100. That’s a quarter of the cost of the only other USB-C charging e-bike on the market.

Sources indicate that of course, it’s not nearly as technologically advanced as Rivian’s ALSO e-bike. But hey, it’s at least shipping.

And while the Zip is a fun little 16″ wheel folding electric bike in its own right, with a compact design that makes it easy to store and transport, it’s the charging setup that has me particularly excited.

Instead of keeping track of yet another proprietary charging brick, I can simply grab the USB-C charger from my laptop and plug it into the bike. There’s one in my living room by the couch. There’s one by my bed. There’s one in all of my friends’ places. There’s a USB-C charger everywhere.

If I’m traveling around, that means one less charger to pack. If I’m visiting someone, there’s a decent chance they already have a compatible charger sitting around.

Heck, I can even use a basic USB-C phone charger in a pinch. Sure, charging a relatively large e-bike battery at 20W isn’t going to be particularly quick, but the fact that I can do it at all is incredibly convenient.

Plus, the bike has one more trick. The battery also outputs USB-C, so I can charge my laptop or other devices from it as well. I can even charge two devices simultaneously, thanks to the dual USB-C ports.

Sources indicate that the battery is housed in a roll-top bag that is locked into the headset of the bike but can be swiftly unlocked for charging off the bike. And since it’s a keyed lock, no one can steal the battery even when the bag is left on the bike.

I typically charge the battery still mounted on the bike, though occasionally when I want to use a friend’s USB-C charger, I’ll just pop the bag off and bring it right up to wherever the closest USB-C charger is located.

It may not be the fastest charge, but it’s pretty darn convenient. And with a 360Wh battery, a powerful 100W laptop charger will still get it pretty much full in 4 hours, or for a more typical 50% recharge, roughly two hours.

And that’s really the beauty of USB-C charging. It’s not necessarily about charging faster. It’s about having options. It’s about not being stuck if the very specific charger that only works on your e-bike doesn’t happen to be around exactly where you are.

Industry observers note that of course, there’s a technical reason we haven’t seen USB-C charging spread across the e-bike industry quite as quickly as it has with smaller electronics. Most e-bike batteries operate at 36V or 48V nominal, meaning their charging voltages are higher than the 20V typically supplied by common USB-C laptop chargers. That requires additional voltage conversion and charging circuitry inside the bike or battery.

In a recent development, but clearly, it can be done. And if ENGWE can offer it on a €999 electric bike, there’s a pretty compelling argument that more manufacturers should be taking a serious look at the technology. In this case, it’s all housed inside the battery, meaning it could be directly incorporated into any e-bike whose manufacturer is brave enough to spec it.

USB-C charging aside, there's a very good reason that just about every folding e-bike on the market has put thick plates on the folding connection of the frame. It's because the frame breaks if they're not there. Just like this one is going to.

In a recent development, I’m not suggesting that every e-bike needs to abandon its dedicated charger tomorrow. For larger batteries, high-powered chargers still make plenty of sense, especially when you want to get back on the road quickly.

Sources indicate that but having USB-C as an additional charging option? That’s something I’d love to see become standard.

For years, we’ve seen how electric bikes are becoming more convenient, more practical, and better integrated into our everyday lives. Yet when it comes to charging, we’re still carrying around a collection of more or less proprietary chargers.

Recent findings suggest that now I’m riding a barely $1k electric bike that can charge from the same power brick as my laptop. And frankly, I think it’s about time the rest of the e-bike industry caught up!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SUMMER MAY BE behind us, but that doesn’t mean your swim trunks need to go into hibernation. If you’re planning to escape the cold for somewhere sunny this winter, a good pair should be in your suitcase. The beauty of men’s swim trunks is that they can be worn in or out of the water, doubling as the ultimate beachside bottoms or everyday shorts. The best swim trunks for men today have a moisture-wicking and quick-drying fabric, four-way stretch for mobility, a flattering length, and an athletic fit. Finding the right one for you can be a challenge, which is why we're here to help. Our team of fashion editors spent the past year trying and testing swim trunks to find options that blend comfort and style.

Recent findings suggest that over the past four years, I’ve tested more than 20 different pairs of swim trunks—everything from legacy surf brands to buzzy newcomers—but Fair Harbor’s have consistently exceeded my expectations. This pair nails that trifecta of being stylish, functional, and worth the price.

The first thing I noticed: the fabric. It’s a cotton-poly blend that feels smooth and broken-in right out of the gate. It doesn’t feel like any of that stiff, swishy, overly synthetic feel you get with most swim trunks. I’m usually quick to write off built-in liners altogether, but the BreezeKnit liner changed my mind. It feels more like a supportive pair of boxer briefs than the usual scratchy mesh. It’s snug (but comfortable on the crown jewels), breathable, and, most importantly, it doesn’t ride up or chafe. I’ve worn it for full beach days in Puerto Rico—swimming, walking, grabbing lunch—and never once felt the need to adjust.

Sources indicate that the 7-inch inseam hits just above the knee on me, giving it a clean, tailored look. It’s an easy middle ground that works whether you’re getting in the water or just wearing it as your default summer short. There’s enough stretch in the cotton-polyester fabric that I never feel restricted. Plus, it comes in seersucker versions, solid-colored options, and other unique patterns. The hidden zipper pocket stashes a key or card without them slipping out, and the side pockets don’t balloon up in the water—something a lot of trunks still get wrong. It’s not a substitute for a gym short, but the fabric dries quickly for other oceanside activities.

I can’t get enough of the R&R Trunk's timeless style, functional fabric, and flattering fit. I love the no-fuss design with a tailored cut that’s not too baggy or slim. Coupled with the flexible waistband, the fit looks great on most body types. It’s available in two inseams–5.5 and 7.5 inches. The latter provides enough coverage and hits a couple inches above the knee for most men (our universal style recommendation for shorts). Though I wore the shorter length on the beach during my stay in Miami because it highlights off my summer leg gains.

Rhone’s athleisure performs just as well as it looks. I’ve sweat-tested the R&R during beachside runs and volleyball games, and found that its odor-fighting fabric kept me feeling fresh. The mesh liner kept my family jewels locked in, without cutting off circulation. A few editors on our style team who have the R&R trunk say that the liner really does have a second-skin like quality. That’s probably because the polyester blend fabric is stretchy, which felt more comfortable than Lululemon’s (also great!) Swim Short. These durable features also mean the R&R Trunk doubles as a decent gym short if you’re in a pinch, and saves you one less thing to pack for a tropical vacation. We love that it comes in 11 colorways, but if you want to go classic, you can’t go wrong with the Electric Blue or Navy option.

The absence of liner offers a comfortable commando style, which is why I prefer a pair like this one from Lululemon. I don’t have to be bothered with any mesh material that feels restrictive or scratchy against my crown jewels—I can just slip it on and head into the water. I also love that the minimal design doesn’t scream “swim trunk”, so I can go from brunch to the boardwalk or the pool without having to do an outfit change. It passes as an everyday short, which is exactly the kind of versatility I want in the summer. The polyester-elastomultiester fabric has so much stretch, it performs just as good—if not better—than most of my gym shorts.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve worn this pair for pickup volleyball and quick workouts, and they move with you instead of clinging or sagging out. It also dries fast and doesn't get that heavy, waterlogged feel after a swim, which makes a huge difference if you’re posted up poolside for a while. The 7-inch inseam is short enough to show some quad, but long enough that it still feels put-together if you’re grabbing a drink after. On my 5’8” frame, it lands a couple inches above the knee with a clean, tailored look—not too baggy, not too slim. If you’re taller, it’ll read a bit shorter and sportier; shorter guys get that ideal mid-thigh cut without going full retro.

After testing Proof’s Performance Swim Trunk, we found that it’s easily the most durable short on this list. Our editors appreciate the polyester-spandex blend fabric, which is stretchy, quick drying, and nearly tear proof. We’ve sported this during tropical hikes and extreme water sports, and found that the Performance Trunk held up to just about anything mother nature threw at it. We like the moisture-wicking liner, which is actually more comfortable than Rhone’s R&R short, but we did find it didn’t dry as promptly as Rhone’s short, and is a bit thicker than we’d prefer. Still, those are minor quibbles for a swim trunk as functional as this one.

Looks-wise, the Performance Trunk isn’t the most stylish of the bunch, and it’s not meant to be. It’s available in six solid colors and two inseam options, all of which have a no-frills design. Though we have to say, because of its barebones aesthetics, the Performance Trunk looks a lot cleaner than your typical bulky hiking short. Proof markets this as a multipurpose trunk that doubles as a gym short, and after putting it through the paces, we agree with that claim. While it’s not as breathable as Ten Thousand’s award-winning Interval Short, Proof’s stretchy fabric moves easily through all sorts of workouts.

Sources indicate that for your next vacation, you need a dressy swim trunk that can look great at the beach, bar, or restaurant. Enter this one from Bather, which has a plaid-like pattern with complementing tones of maroon and blue. This makes it more polished than your typical swim shorts, so you can easily pair it with a simple polo or the brand’s matching camp shirt and sandals for a foolproof, lunchtime fit in your arsenal. I’ve worn it to a five-star hotel’s restaurant and then straight to the pool for a mid-day cocktail.

The waistband rests gently on the waist, but you can adjust the fit using the drawstrings. Unlike the scratchy net-like liners in cheaper swim trunks, the nylon-spandex blend is silky and irritation-free, so I could wear it for hours and be comfortable. Plus, the 5.5-inch inseam flatters tall and short guys alike. In terms of functionality, the pockets are super deep for your sunglasses or wallet, while one in the back snaps shut for extra security.

Fair Harbor offers so many great trunks, we couldn't help but to feature the Anchor Short, too. It's available in a variety of solids and prints, but we're big fans of the red stripe option, since it has a cool ‘80s vibe that pairs well with laidback T-shirts, tank tops, and more. This style also comes with the BreezeKnit liner—Fair Harbor's soft, supportive alternative to traditional mesh liner found in swimwear. It provides a snug and comfortable feel, while keeping you cool as ice.

Unlike other picks on this list, The Anchor Trunk is available in three inseams. The 6-inch inseam is great for guys who want to show off their hard-earned leg gains this summer. The 8-inch inseam hits the sweet spot between casual and polished, a safe bet if you're unsure which to go for. And the 10-inch inseam is the longest option, ideal for those who prefer a bit more coverage. Plus, its relaxed (not baggy) fit keeps this from veering into Reno 911! territory.

I’ve worn it for early runs along the boardwalk, knocked out quick leg circuits on vacation, and then jumped straight into the water without needing to change. The 5.75-inch inseam gives it a shorter, more athletic cut that feels mobile and unrestrictive, especially when you’re moving. According to recent reports, it’s made from a lightweight polyester-elastane blend that dries promptly and has just enough stretch that you can bend down or twist at any turn. And because the silhouette is sleek and the design is minimal—save for that signature embroidered pony—it pairs easily with a tee or button-down, making it a true wear-all-day option for beach trips, resort hangs, or any summer day that doesn’t stick to one lane.

In a recent development, if you’re looking for something more surf-specific, the California-based brand best known for its laid-back, surfer aesthetic delivers the Cruise Boardshort. The scalloped leg—where the hem curves slightly upward at the outer thigh—gives you a greater range of motion and a subtle retro-sport look. It’s one of those design tweaks that looks cool but also improves mobility.

Recent findings suggest that it’s built to stay put. It’s a small but clutch feature if you’re actually swimming, surfing, or doing anything more active than lounging.

It’s stylish enough to stand out amongst a sea of guys in basic trunks. Like Vuori’s option, this pair falls right above the knee, providing more coverage in case your shorts ride up as you get out of the water. I’m 5'8" and the 18-inch outseam fits pretty long on me, so the fit is more flattering for taller guys around 6’ feet.
